<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:first-main}
For every cyclic extension $K/F$ of prime degree, every 
quasi-character $\chi_F$ of $F^\times$, and every nontrivial
additive character $\psi_F$ of $F$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:first-main}
 \Delta_K(\chi_K,\psi_K)
 \prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\Delta_F(\mu,\psi_F)
 =
 \prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\Delta_F(\mu\chi_F,\psi_F).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Write $p=\operatorname{char}k_E$.  Thus either
$\operatorname{char}E=0$ with residue characteristic $p$, or
$\operatorname{char}E=p$.  An integer occurring in an identity inside
$E$ denotes its image under $\mathbf Z\to E$; in particular $p=0$ in
equal characteristic $p$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The conductor exponent $m_E(\theta)$ is the least $m\ge0$ for which
$\theta$ is trivial on $U_E^m$.  Thus $m_E(\theta)=0$ precisely when
$\theta$ is unramified.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
For a nontrivial additive character $\psi$, the integer $n_E(\psi)$
is characterized by the condition that $\mathfrak p_E^{-n_E(\psi)}$ is the
largest fractional ideal on which $\psi$ is trivial.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite-local-realization}
The summand just defined is well defined.
There is a positive real number $c_m$, depending only on the chosen Haar
measure and $m$, such that
\begin{equation*}
 \int_{U_E^0}\psi(u/\gamma)\theta(u)^{-1}\,du
 =c_m G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma).
\end{equation*}
Moreover
\[
 G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)\ne0.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-finite-realization}
 \Delta_E(\theta,\psi)
 =\theta(\gamma)\operatorname{ph}\bigl(G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and the zero branch in the definition of $\operatorname{ph}$ is never used for a
local constant.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
If $u/v\in U_E^m$, then $\theta(u)=\theta(v)$ and
$u-v\in\mathfrak p_E^m$.  By \eqref{eq:admissible-gamma},
$(u-v)/\gamma\in\mathfrak p_E^{-n}$, so
$\psi(u/\gamma)=\psi(v/\gamma)$.  Thus the summand descends to
$Q_m$.  The integrand is constant on every coset of $U_E^m$ in
$U_E^0$, and all such cosets have the same positive measure $c_m$;
this proves the stated integral formula.

It remains to prove nonvanishing.  If $m=0$, the quotient $Q_0$ is a
singleton and $G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)=1$.
Assume $m>0$ and put $A=\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak p_E^m$.  The pairing
\[
 A\times A\longrightarrow\mathbf C^\times,
 \qquad
 (\bar x,\bar y)\longmapsto\psi(xy/\gamma)
\]
is perfect.  Indeed, its annihilator in either variable is exactly
$\mathfrak p_E^m$: this follows from \eqref{eq:admissible-gamma} and the
maximality of $\mathfrak p_E^{-n}$ in the definition of $n_E(\psi)$.

Extend the function $u\mapsto\theta(u)^{-1}$ on $A^\times$ by zero
to a function $f:A\to\mathbf C$, and write
\[
 \widehat f(x)=
 \sum_{u\in A^\times}\theta(u)^{-1}\psi(xu/\gamma).
\]
Then $\widehat f(1)=G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)$.  If $x\in A^\times$,
the substitution $u\mapsto x^{-1}u$ gives
\begin{equation*}
 \widehat f(x)=\theta(x)\widehat f(1).
\end{equation*}
If $x$ is not a unit, exactness of the conductor provides
$a\in U_E^{m-1}$ with $\theta(a)\ne1$.  Since
$x(a-1)u/\gamma\in\mathfrak p_E^{-n}$ for every $u\in U_E^0$, multiplication
by $a$ permutes $A^\times$ and gives
\[
 \widehat f(x)=\theta(a)^{-1}\widehat f(x),
\]
whence $\widehat f(x)=0$.  If $\widehat f(1)$ were zero,
the formula for the Fourier coefficients at units and the preceding vanishing
would make every Fourier coefficient of $f$ zero.  Perfect finite
Fourier duality would then give $f=0$, contradicting $f(1)=1$.
Thus $G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)\ne0$.  Finally the positive
factor $c_m$ does not change phase, proving
\eqref{eq:delta-finite-realization}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:local-gauss-integral-nonzero}
For every quasi-character $\theta$ and every nontrivial additive
character $\psi$, the integral in \eqref{eq:def-delta} is nonzero.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:gamma-independent}
The right side of \eqref{eq:def-delta} is independent of the choice of
$\gamma$ satisfying \eqref{eq:admissible-gamma}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\gamma'=a\gamma$ with $a\in U_E^0$.  Multiplication by $a$
permutes $Q_m$, and \eqref{eq:finite-local-gauss-sum} gives
\[
 G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma')
 =\theta(a)^{-1}G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma).
\]
The restriction of $\theta$ to $U_E^0$ factors through the finite group
$Q_m$, so $|\theta(a)|=1$.  By nonvanishing,
\[
 \operatorname{ph}\bigl(G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma')\bigr)
 =\theta(a)^{-1}
  \operatorname{ph}\bigl(G_E(\theta,\psi;\gamma)\bigr).
\]
Since $\theta(\gamma')=\theta(a)\theta(\gamma)$, the two factors
cancel.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:residual-normalization}
Let $\psi_F$ have conductor exponent $n$, and fix a uniformizer
$\varpi_F$.  The formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-additive-character}
 \bar\psi(\bar x)
 =\psi_F(x\varpi_F^{-n-1}),
 \qquad x\in\mathcal O_F\text{ a lift of }\bar x\in k_F,
\end{equation}
defines a nontrivial additive character of $k_F$, independently of the
choice of the lift $x$.  Define the canonical additive character
$\psi_{\rm can}:k_F\to\mathbf C^\times$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-additive-parametrization}
 x\longmapsto
 \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{p}
   \operatorname{Tr}_{k_F/\mathbf F_p}(x)\right).
\end{equation}
Then there is a unit $a\in\mathcal O_F^\times$ such that the residual
character attached to $\psi_F^a(x)=\psi_F(ax)$ is $\psi_{\rm can}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Well-definedness follows because two lifts differ by an element of
$\mathfrak p_F$, and therefore their arguments differ by an element of
$\mathfrak p_F^{-n}$, on which $\psi_F$ is trivial.  Nontriviality follows
from the maximality of $\mathfrak p_F^{-n}$.  Since the trace pairing
$k_F\times k_F\to\mathbf F_p$ is nondegenerate, there is a unique
$c\in k_F^\times$ such that
$\bar\psi(x)=\psi_{\rm can}(cx)$.  Choose a unit $a\in\mathcal O_F^\times$
with residue $c^{-1}$; then the residual character attached to
$\psi_F^a$ is $\psi_{\rm can}$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:additive-scale}
For $a\in E^\times$, put $\psi^a(x)=\psi(ax)$.  Then
\begin{equation*}
 \Delta_E(\theta,\psi^a)
 =\theta(a)\Delta_E(\theta,\psi).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If $v_E(a)=r$, then $n_E(\psi^a)=n_E(\psi)+r$.  Hence $a\gamma$ is
admissible for $(\theta,\psi^a)$ whenever $\gamma$ is admissible for
$(\theta,\psi)$, and
$\psi^a(u/(a\gamma))=\psi(u/\gamma)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:additive-independence}
For every $a\in F^\times$, the First Main Lemma for $\psi_F$ is
equivalent to the First Main Lemma for $\psi_F^a$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:prime-norm-characters}, the group $S(K/F)$ has
$\ell$ elements.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-scale}, the two sides of \eqref{eq:first-main} acquire
the respective factors
\[
 \chi_K(a)\prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\mu(a)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \chi_F(a)^\ell\prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\mu(a).
\]
Since $N_{K/F}(a)=a^\ell$ for $a\in F^\times$, these factors agree.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:delta-one}
For every nontrivial additive character $\psi$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trivial-local-constant}
 \Delta_E(1,\psi)=1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Here $m_E(1)=0$.  Formula
\eqref{eq:unramified-character-local-constant} gives the result.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:inverse-pair}
Let $\mu$ be a finite-order character of $E^\times$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inverse-pair}
 \Delta_E(\mu,\psi)\Delta_E(\mu^{-1},\psi)=\mu(-1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Choose a common admissible $\gamma$ and write
\[
 I_\mu=\int_{U_E^0}\psi(u/\gamma)\mu(u)^{-1}\,du.
\]
Both $I_\mu$ and $I_{\mu^{-1}}$ are nonzero by
Corollary~\ref{cor:local-gauss-integral-nonzero}.  Since $\mu$ and
$\psi$ are unitary,
\[
 \overline{I_\mu}
 =\int_{U_E^0}\psi(-u/\gamma)\mu(u)\,du
 =\mu(-1)I_{\mu^{-1}}.
\]
The product of the two phases is therefore $\mu(-1)^{-1}=\mu(-1)$,
and the factors $\mu(\gamma)$ and $\mu^{-1}(\gamma)$ cancel.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:S-product-one}
If $K/F$ is cyclic of odd prime degree, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-product-one}
 \prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\Delta_F(\mu,\psi_F)=1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The finiteness of $S(K/F)$ follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:prime-norm-characters}.  For $x\in F^\times$,
viewed as an element of $K^\times$, one has
$N_{K/F}(x)=x^\ell$.  Hence, for every $\mu\in S(K/F)$,
\[
 \mu(x)^\ell=\mu(N_{K/F}(x))=1.
\]
Thus every nontrivial $\mu$ has order $\ell$, which is odd, and in
particular $\mu(-1)=1$.  Apply \eqref{eq:inverse-pair} to each pair
$\mu,\mu^{-1}$ and \eqref{eq:trivial-local-constant} to the trivial character.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:error-term}
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=
 \frac{\Delta_K(\chi_K,\psi_K)
       \prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\Delta_F(\mu,\psi_F)}
      {\prod_{\mu\in S(K/F)}\Delta_F(\mu\chi_F,\psi_F)}.
\end{equation}
The denominator is nonzero by
Corollary~\ref{cor:local-gauss-integral-nonzero}, and the First Main
Lemma is the assertion $\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=1$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:twist-invariance}
For every $\nu\in S(K/F)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:error-twist-invariance}
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\nu\chi_F)=\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $\nu\circ N_{K/F}=1$, the character on $K^\times$ is unchanged.
Multiplication by $\nu$ permutes the group $S(K/F)$, including its
trivial character, so the denominator is only reindexed.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:minimal-orbit-reduction}
To prove Theorem~\ref{thm:first-main}, it is enough, for each
$S(K/F)$-orbit of quasi-characters, to prove
$\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=1$ for one member of minimal multiplicative
conductor.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The conductors in an orbit are nonnegative integers, so a minimum
exists.  Equation~\eqref{eq:error-twist-invariance} shows that
$\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)$ is constant on each orbit.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:graded-norm}\label{thm:norm-filtration}
Let $K/F$ be ramified cyclic of prime degree $\ell$, with lower break
$t$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The different exponent is
\[
 D_{K/F}=(\ell-1)(t+1),
\]
and for every integer $a$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trace-ideal}
 \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\mathfrak p_K^a)=
 \mathfrak p_F^{\left\lfloor(a+D_{K/F})/\ell\right\rfloor}.
\end{equation}

\item For $0\le i\le t$, let
\[
 \overline N_i:\operatorname{gr}^iU_K\longrightarrow
                   \operatorname{gr}^iU_F,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{gr}^iU_E=U_E^i/U_E^{i+1},
\]
be the map induced by the norm.  For $0\le i<t$ it is an isomorphism.
At $i=t$, its kernel and cokernel both have order $\ell$, and its
kernel is the image of $G_t/G_{t+1}$ under the ramification map
\[
 \sigma\longmapsto
 \begin{cases}
  \overline{\sigma(\varpi_K)/\varpi_K},&t=0,\\[1mm]
  \overline{(\sigma(\varpi_K)-\varpi_K)/\varpi_K^{t+1}},&t>0.
 \end{cases}
\]

\item Splicing the graded maps below the break gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm-below-break}
 K^\times/U_K^t\xrightarrow{\sim}F^\times/U_F^t,
 \qquad
 U_K^r/U_K^t\xrightarrow{\sim}U_F^r/U_F^t
 \quad(0\le r\le t).
\end{equation}
\item For every integer $r>t$, put
$a=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)$.  The norm induces an isomorphism
\[
 U_K^a/U_K^{a+1}\longrightarrow U_F^r/U_F^{r+1}.
\]
Moreover, for every $a\ge0$, the subgroup $N_{K/F}(U_K^a)$ is closed in
$U_F^0$, and consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm-above-break}
 N_{K/F}(U_K^{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)})=U_F^r,
 \qquad
 N_{K/F}(U_K^{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)+1})=U_F^{r+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Choose a uniformizer $\varpi_K$.  For every $\sigma\ne1$ one has
$v_K(\sigma(\varpi_K)-\varpi_K)=t+1$.  The different formula
\[
 v_K(\mathfrak D_{K/F})
 =\sum_{\sigma\ne1}v_K(\sigma(\varpi_K)-\varpi_K),
\]
which is \cite[Chapter~IV, \S1, Proposition~4]{Serre}, gives the first
assertion in (a).

For the trace formula, the trace-dual of $\mathfrak p_K^a$ under
$(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(xy)$ is
$\mathfrak p_K^{-a-D_{K/F}}$ by
\cite[Chapter~III, \S3, Proposition~7]{Serre}.  Write
$\operatorname{Tr}(\mathfrak p_K^a)=\mathfrak p_F^c$.  An element $y\in F$ belongs to the dual of
this trace ideal if and only if
\[
 y\mathfrak p_K^a\subseteq\mathfrak p_K^{-D_{K/F}},
 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
 \ell v_F(y)+a\ge-D_{K/F}.
\]
Thus its dual is
$\mathfrak p_F^{\lceil(-a-D_{K/F})/\ell\rceil}$, whereas the dual of
$\mathfrak p_F^c$ is $\mathfrak p_F^{-c}$.  Hence
\[
 c=\left\lfloor\frac{a+D_{K/F}}\ell\right\rfloor,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:trace-ideal}.

The graded maps in (b), including the critical kernel, are the
cyclic-prime specialization of
\cite[Chapter~V, \S3, Propositions~4--5]{Serre}.  For (c), splice the
graded isomorphisms for $0\le i<t$.  The valuation quotient is preserved
because the residue degree is one:
$v_F(N_{K/F}x)=v_K(x)$.  If $t=0$, then
$K^\times/U_K^0\simeq\mathbf Z$ and norm is the identity on the
valuation quotient.  If $t>0$, the residue norm
$U_K^0/U_K^1\to U_F^0/U_F^1$ is $x\mapsto x^\ell=x^p$, hence is
Frobenius, and the remaining graded pieces below $t$ are isomorphisms.
This proves \eqref{eq:norm-below-break}.

For (d), the above-break graded isomorphism is
\cite[Chapter~V, \S3, Corollaries~1--3]{Serre}.  Each $U_K^a$ is
compact, so $N_{K/F}(U_K^a)$ is compact and hence closed in $U_F^0$.
Successive lifting through the graded isomorphisms therefore converges
to a norm and gives \eqref{eq:norm-above-break}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:frobenius-difference-trace}
Let $k/\mathbf F_p$ be a finite field extension and let
$\lambda\in k^\times$.  Then the $\mathbf F_p$-linear maps
\[
 \wp(z)=z^p-z,
 \qquad
 \wp_\lambda(z)=z^p-\lambda^{p-1}z
\]
satisfy
\[
 \ker(\wp)=\mathbf F_p,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{im}(\wp)=\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_p}\right),
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scaled-frobenius-trace-image}
 \ker(\wp_\lambda)=\lambda\mathbf F_p,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{im}(\wp_\lambda)
 =\lambda^p\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_p}\right).
\end{equation}
Under the perfect trace pairing $(a,x)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_p}(ax)$, the
annihilator of the last image is $\lambda^{-p}\mathbf F_p$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The kernel of $\wp$ is the prime field.  Hence its image has
$\mathbf F_p$-dimension $[k:\mathbf F_p]-1$.  Frobenius invariance of the trace gives
$\operatorname{Tr}(z^p-z)=0$, so the image is contained in the trace-zero hyperplane;
the two spaces have the same dimension and therefore coincide.  Since
\[
 \wp_\lambda(\lambda y)=\lambda^p(y^p-y),
\]
the scaled kernel and image follow.  The orthogonal complement of
$\ker(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_p})$ is $\mathbf F_p$: it contains $\mathbf F_p$, and both  have
dimension one.  Scaling the second variable by $\lambda^p$ gives the
annihilator $\lambda^{-p}\mathbf F_p$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:critical-norm-polynomial}
Let $K/F$ be totally ramified cyclic of prime degree
$p=\operatorname{char}k_F$, with positive lower break $t$, and identify
the residue fields with $k$.
Choose a uniformizer $\varpi_K$, put
$\varpi_F=N_{K/F}(\varpi_K)$, choose a generator $\sigma$ of
$\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$, and set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-ramification-coordinate}
 \lambda=
 \overline{\frac{\sigma(\varpi_K)-\varpi_K}
                   {\varpi_K^{t+1}}}\in k^\times.
\end{equation}
For $z,w\in k$, let $\widetilde z,\widetilde w\in\mathcal O_F\subset\mathcal O_K$
be any lifts.  We use the standard identifications
\[
 \operatorname{gr}^tU_K=U_K^t/U_K^{t+1}\simeq(k,+),
 \qquad
 (1+\varpi_K^t\widetilde z)U_K^{t+1}\longleftrightarrow z,
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{gr}^tU_F=U_F^t/U_F^{t+1}\simeq(k,+),
 \qquad
 (1+\varpi_F^t\widetilde w)U_F^{t+1}\longleftrightarrow w.
\]
In these source and target coordinates, the critical graded norm is the
additive polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-norm-polynomial-extracted}
 P_\lambda(Z)=Z^p-\lambda^{p-1}Z.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-norm-image}
 \ker P_\lambda=\lambda\mathbf F_p,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{im}P_\lambda
 =\lambda^p\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_p}\right),
\end{equation}
and its annihilator under the trace pairing is
$\lambda^{-p}\mathbf F_p$.  The linear coefficient is the normalized trace:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-norm-trace-coefficient}
 \overline{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t)}{\varpi_F^t}}
 =-\lambda^{p-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $2\le j\le p-1$, let $s_j$ be the $j$th elementary symmetric
function of the conjugates of $\varpi_K^t$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:wild-symmetric-bound} gives
\[
 v_F(s_j)\ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{jt+(p-1)(t+1)}p\right\rfloor
 \ge t+1,
\]
since $(j-1)t\ge1$.  There are no such terms when $p=2$.
The trace-ideal formula \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} gives
$\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t)\in\mathfrak p_F^t$, while
\[
 N_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t\widetilde z)=\varpi_F^t\widetilde z^{\,p}.
\]
Thus the norm expansion gives
\[
 N_{K/F}(1+\varpi_K^t\widetilde z)
 \equiv1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t)\widetilde z
          +\varpi_F^t\widetilde z^{\,p}
 \pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{t+1}}.
\]
The critical norm map is therefore represented by $Z^p+aZ$, where
\[
 a=\overline{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t)}{\varpi_F^t}}.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:graded-norm}(b), its kernel is
$\lambda\mathbf F_p$.  In particular $\lambda^p+a\lambda=0$; since
$\lambda\ne0$, this gives $a=-\lambda^{p-1}$.
This proves \eqref{eq:critical-norm-polynomial-extracted} and
\eqref{eq:critical-norm-trace-coefficient}.
The kernel, image, and annihilator assertions follow from
Lemma~\ref{lem:frobenius-difference-trace}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:wild-symmetric-bound}
Assume that $K/F$ is wildly ramified cyclic of prime degree
$\ell=p=\operatorname{char}k_F$, with lower break $t$, and put
$T=t+1$.
For $x\in K$ let $s_j(x)$ be the $j$th elementary symmetric function
of its $p$ conjugates.  If $v_K(x)\ge a$, then, for
$1\le j\le p-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symmetric-bound}
 v_F(s_j(x))\ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{ja+(p-1)T}{p}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
For the last coefficient,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symmetric-bound-last}
 v_F(s_p(x))=v_F(N_{K/F}x)=v_K(x)\ge a.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Put $D=D_{K/F}=v_K(\mathfrak D_{K/F})$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:norm-filtration}(a),
$D=(p-1)T$.  Put $P_i(x)=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(x^i)$.  Since
$x^i\in\mathfrak p_K^{ia}$, equation
\eqref{eq:trace-ideal} gives
\begin{equation*}
 v_F(P_i(x))\ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{ia+D}{p}\right\rfloor
 \qquad(i\ge1).
\end{equation*}
We now use Newton's identities
\begin{equation*}
 j s_j(x)=\sum_{i=1}^j(-1)^{i-1}s_{j-i}(x)P_i(x),
 \qquad s_0(x)=1.
\end{equation*}
Because $j<p$, the integer $j$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_F$.  We prove
\eqref{eq:symmetric-bound} by induction on $j$.  For $j=1$ it is
equation~\eqref{eq:trace-ideal}, applied to $x$.  Suppose it is known below $j$.
The term $i=j$ in Newton's identity has the required
valuation by \eqref{eq:trace-ideal}, applied to $x^j$.
For $i<j$, the induction hypothesis and \eqref{eq:trace-ideal},
applied to $x^i$, give
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{(j-i)a+D}{p}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{ia+D}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
For real numbers $A,B$ one has
$\lfloor A\rfloor+\lfloor B\rfloor\ge\lfloor A+B\rfloor-1$.
Here the sum before taking floors is
\[
 \frac{ja+D}{p}+\frac Dp.
\]
The extension is wild, so $T\ge2$ and
$D/p=(p-1)T/p\ge1$.  Hence the last displayed integral lower bound is
at least $\lfloor(ja+D)/p\rfloor$.  Every term in
Newton's identity therefore has the required valuation.
Finally $s_p(x)=N_{K/F}(x)$, and total ramification gives
$v_F(N_{K/F}x)=v_K(x)$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:wild-norm-truncation}
Let $q,r\ge0$ and assume
\begin{equation*}
 2q+(p-1)T\ge pr.
\end{equation*}
Then, for every $y\in\mathfrak p_K^q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wild-norm-truncation}
 N_{K/F}(1+y)
 \equiv1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)+N_{K/F}(y)
 \pmod{\mathfrak p_F^r}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For $2\le j\le p-1$, Equation~\eqref{eq:symmetric-bound} gives
\[
 v_F(s_j(y))\ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{jq+(p-1)T}{p}\right\rfloor
 \ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{2q+(p-1)T}{p}\right\rfloor\ge r.
\]
The norm expansion then gives
\eqref{eq:wild-norm-truncation}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:stable-critical-trace}
Let $K/F$ be totally ramified cyclic of odd prime degree $p$, with
positive lower break $t$.  Choose a uniformizer $\varpi_K$ and a generator $\sigma$ of
$\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$, put $\varpi_F=N_{K/F}(\varpi_K)$, and define $\lambda$ by
\eqref{eq:critical-ramification-coordinate}.  Suppose $d\ge t+1$
and put
\[
 d'=pd-\frac{p-1}{2}t.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\varpi_F}{\varpi_K^p}
 \equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak p_K^{t+1}},
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
 \varpi_K^{2d'}
 \equiv \varpi_F^{2d-t}\varpi_K^t
 \pmod{\mathfrak p_K^{2d'+1}},
\end{equation*}
and
the normalized traces are units with common residue
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-trace-residue}
 \overline{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^{2d'})}{\varpi_F^{2d}}}
 =\overline{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^t)}{\varpi_F^t}}
 =-\lambda^{p-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
For $j\in\mathbf F_p$, put
\[
 a_j=\frac{\sigma^j(\varpi_K)}{\varpi_K}-1.
\]
The ramification homomorphism gives $a_j\in\mathfrak p_K^t$ and
$\overline{a_j/\varpi_K^t}=j\lambda$.  Products of at least two of the
$a_j$ lie in $\mathfrak p_K^{t+1}$, and $\sum_{j\in\mathbf F_p}j=0$.  Hence
\[
 \frac{\varpi_F}{\varpi_K^p}
 =\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p}(1+a_j)
 \equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak p_K^{t+1}},
\]
which proves the first congruence.  Since
$2d'=p(2d-t)+t$, raising the inverse ratio to the power $2d-t$ and
multiplying by $\varpi_K^t$ gives
the second congruence.

The trace-ideal formula \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} sends the difference in
the second congruence into $\mathfrak p_F^{2d+1}$.
After division by $\varpi_F^{2d}$, the normalized traces have equal
residues.  In the critical source
coordinate the linear coefficient of the graded norm is
$\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(\varpi_K^t)/\varpi_F^t}$.  Proposition
\ref{prop:critical-norm-polynomial} identifies it with
$-\lambda^{p-1}$, which is nonzero.  This proves
\eqref{eq:stable-critical-trace-residue} and the unit assertions.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:additive-conductor}
Let $\psi_K=\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}$.  If $K/F$ is totally ramified of
degree $\ell$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:additive-conductor-trace}
 n_K(\psi_K)=\ell n_F(\psi_F)+D_{K/F}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The largest fractional ideal $I$ on which $\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}$ is trivial
is characterized by $\operatorname{Tr}(I)\subseteq\mathfrak p_F^{-n_F(\psi_F)}$.  By the trace
duality used in the proof of \eqref{eq:trace-ideal}, this ideal is
$\mathfrak p_K^{-\ell n_F(\psi_F)-D_{K/F}}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:norm-characters}
Let $K/F$ be ramified cyclic of prime degree $\ell$.  Then
$F^\times/N_{K/F}(K^\times)$ is cyclic of order $\ell$, the group
$S(K/F)$ has $\ell$ elements, and every nontrivial
$\mu\in S(K/F)$ has conductor exponent $t+1$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.
The first isomorphism in \eqref{eq:norm-below-break} shows that
\[
 F^\times=N(K^\times)U_F^t.
\]
Its injectivity also shows that
\[
 N(K^\times)\cap U_F^t=N(U_K^t).
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation*}
 F^\times/N(K^\times)\simeq U_F^t/N(U_K^t).
\end{equation*}
Taking $r=t+1$ in \eqref{eq:norm-above-break} gives
\[
 U_F^{t+1}=N(U_K^{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(t+1)})\subseteq N(U_K^t),
\]
because $\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(t+1)>t$.  Hence
\[
 U_F^t/N(U_K^t)
 \simeq
 \operatorname{coker}\left(
 U_K^t/U_K^{t+1}\longrightarrow U_F^t/U_F^{t+1}
 \right).
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:norm-filtration}(b), this cokernel has order
$\ell$.  Thus $F^\times/N(K^\times)$ has order $\ell$, and is
cyclic because $\ell$ is prime.

By \eqref{eq:norm-above-break}, $U_F^{t+1}\subseteq N(K^\times)$,
so $N(K^\times)$ is open and the quotient is discrete.  The elements
of $S(K/F)$ are therefore exactly the complex characters of this cyclic
quotient.  A
character is determined by the image of a generator, which may be any
$\ell$th root of unity.  Hence $S(K/F)$ has $\ell$ elements.

The identification $F^\times/N(K^\times)\simeq U_F^t/N(U_K^t)$ shows that
$U_F^t$ maps onto the norm quotient, whereas $U_F^{t+1}$ maps to the
identity.  A nontrivial norm character is therefore nontrivial on
$U_F^t$ and trivial on $U_F^{t+1}$.  Its conductor exponent is exactly
$t+1$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:pullback-conductor}
Let $K/F$ be ramified cyclic of prime degree $\ell$, with break $t$.
Let $m=m_F(\chi_F)$ and $m'=m_K(\chi_F\circ N_{K/F})$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $m>t+1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pullback-high}
 m'-1=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(m-1).
\end{equation}
\item If $m\leq t$, then $m'=m$.
\item If $m=t+1$, then $m'\leq m$; moreover $m'<m$ if and only if
there is a $\mu\in S(K/F)$ for which
$m_F(\mu\chi_F)<t+1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
For (i), put $a=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(m-1)$.  By
\eqref{eq:norm-above-break}, $N_{K/F}(U_K^{a+1})=U_F^m$ and
$N_{K/F}(U_K^a)=U_F^{m-1}$.  Since $m$ is the exact conductor of $\chi_F$,
the pullback is trivial on $U_K^{a+1}$ and nontrivial on $U_K^a$.
Thus $m'=a+1$, which is \eqref{eq:pullback-high}.

For (ii), first separate $m=0$: an unramified character is trivial on
$U_F^0$, hence its norm pullback is unramified and $m'=0$.  Now assume
$1\le m\le t$.  The character $\chi_F$ is nontrivial on
$U_F^{m-1}/U_F^m$.  The graded norm map is an isomorphism at every
level $<t$, so its pullback is nontrivial on
$U_K^{m-1}/U_K^m$ and trivial on $U_K^m$.  Hence $m'=m$.

For (iii), the pullback is always trivial on $U_K^{t+1}$, so
$m'\le t+1=m$.  It has smaller conductor precisely when the restriction
of $\chi_F$ to the image
\[
 I=\operatorname{im}\bigl(U_K^t/U_K^{t+1}\longrightarrow
                          U_F^t/U_F^{t+1}\bigr)
\]
is trivial.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:norm-filtration}(b), the quotient
$(U_F^t/U_F^{t+1})/I$ has order $\ell$.  The proof of
Corollary~\ref{cor:norm-characters} identifies this quotient with
$F^\times/N_{K/F}(K^\times)$, so its character group is exactly the
restriction of $S(K/F)$ to the last unit layer.  Therefore
$\chi_F|_I=1$ if and only if there is a unique restriction
$\mu|_{U_F^t/U_F^{t+1}}$ with
$(\mu\chi_F)|_{U_F^t/U_F^{t+1}}=1$, equivalently
$m_F(\mu\chi_F)<t+1$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:unramified-compatibility}
Let $K/F$ be an unramified extension of degree $f$, and let $\varpi$ be a
uniformizer of $F$.  Then $\varpi$ is also a uniformizer of $K$,
$[k_K:k_F]=f$, and the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Reduction commutes with trace and norm:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unramified-residue-trace-norm}
 \overline{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(x)}=\operatorname{Tr}_{k_K/k_F}(\bar x)
 \quad(x\in\mathcal O_K),
 \qquad
 \overline{N_{K/F}(u)}=N_{k_K/k_F}(\bar u)
 \quad(u\in\mathcal O_K^\times).
\end{equation}
\item For every integer $a$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unramified-trace-ideal}
 \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\mathfrak p_K^a)=\mathfrak p_F^a.
\end{equation}
\item For every $r\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unramified-norm-units}
 N_{K/F}(U_K^r)=U_F^r,
 \qquad N_{K/F}(\varpi)=\varpi^f.
\end{equation}
\item If $\psi_K=\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}$ and
$\chi_K=\chi_F\circ N_{K/F}$, then
\[
 n_K(\psi_K)=n_F(\psi_F),
 \qquad m_K(\chi_K)=m_F(\chi_F).
\]
\item The quotient $F^\times/N_{K/F}(K^\times)$ is cyclic of order $f$,
generated by the class of $\varpi$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.
Since $K/F$ is unramified, its ramification index is $1$.  Thus
$\mathfrak p_K=\varpi\mathcal O_K$, and the residue extension has degree $f$.
The conjugates of an integral element reduce to the conjugates of its
residue class.  Taking the first and last coefficients of the
characteristic polynomial therefore gives
\eqref{eq:unramified-residue-trace-norm}.

We use two elementary finite-field facts.  The map
$\operatorname{Tr}_{k_K/k_F}$ is onto: if $q=|k_F|$, its polynomial
\[
 X+X^q+\cdots+X^{q^{f-1}}
\]
is nonzero and has degree $q^{f-1}<q^f=|k_K|$, so it cannot vanish on
all of $k_K$; a nonzero $k_F$-linear map to the one-dimensional space
$k_F$ is surjective.  The map $N_{k_K/k_F}:k_K^\times\to k_F^\times$
is onto because $k_K^\times$ is cyclic and
\[
 N_{k_K/k_F}(x)=x^{(q^f-1)/(q-1)}
\]
has image of order $q-1$.

Choose $x\in\mathcal O_K$ whose residue has trace $1$.  Then
$\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(x)$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_F$; after multiplying $x$ by its
inverse, we obtain an integral element of trace $1$.  Hence
$\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\mathcal O_K)=\mathcal O_F$.  Since
$\mathfrak p_K^a=\varpi^a\mathcal O_K$ for every $a\in\mathbf Z$, this proves
\eqref{eq:unramified-trace-ideal}.

For $r\geq1$ and $x\in\mathcal O_K$, multiplication of the conjugates gives
\begin{equation*}
 N(1+\varpi^r x)
 \equiv 1+\varpi^r\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(x)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{r+1}}.
\end{equation*}
Thus the map induced by norm on
$U_K^r/U_K^{r+1}\to U_F^r/U_F^{r+1}$ is the finite-field trace and is
surjective.  Starting with $v\in U_F^r$, choose a lift of its class,
divide $v$ by the norm of that lift, and repeat at levels
$r+1,r+2,\ldots$.  Completeness makes the product of the successive
lifts converge to an element of $U_K^r$ with norm $v$.  This proves
$N(U_K^r)=U_F^r$ for $r\geq1$.  Surjectivity of the finite-field norm,
followed by the case $r=1$, gives $N(U_K^0)=U_F^0$.  Finally, because
$\varpi\in F$, its norm is $\varpi^f$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:unramified-norm-units}.

Put $n=n_F(\psi_F)$.  By \eqref{eq:unramified-trace-ideal},
$\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}$ is trivial on $\mathfrak p_K^{-n}$ and is not trivial on
$\mathfrak p_K^{-n-1}$, so $n_K(\psi_K)=n$.  By
\eqref{eq:unramified-norm-units}, for every $r\geq0$ the character
$\chi_F\circ N$ is trivial on $U_K^r$ if and only if $\chi_F$ is
trivial on $U_F^r$.  Hence the multiplicative conductors are equal.
This proves the conductor equalities in part~(d).

Every $y\in K^\times$ has the form $y=\varpi^a u$ with
$u\in U_K^0$, so
\[
 N(K^\times)=\varpi^{f\mathbf Z}U_F^0
\]
by \eqref{eq:unramified-norm-units}.  The last assertion follows.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:prime-norm-characters}
Let $K/F$ be cyclic of prime degree $\ell$.  Then
$F^\times/N_{K/F}(K^\times)$ is cyclic of order $\ell$, and
$S(K/F)$ has $\ell$ elements.  In particular, $S(K/F)$ is finite.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
If $K/F$ is ramified, this is
Corollary~\ref{cor:norm-characters}.  Suppose that it is unramified.
Lemma~\ref{lem:unramified-compatibility}(e) gives a cyclic norm
quotient of order $\ell$, and
\eqref{eq:unramified-norm-units} shows that the norm group contains the
open subgroup $U_F^0$.  Thus the quotient is discrete, and the remainder
of the proof is the same as in Corollary~\ref{cor:norm-characters}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-duality}
Let $n=n_E(\psi)$, let $M,q,r\in\mathbf Z$ with $r\le q$, and let
$\Gamma\in E^\times$ satisfy
\[
 \Gamma\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^{M+n}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \mathfrak p_E^{M-q}/\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}\ \times\
 \mathfrak p_E^r/\mathfrak p_E^q
 \longrightarrow\mathbf C^\times,
 \qquad(\bar c,\bar x)\longmapsto\psi(cx/\Gamma),
\end{equation*}
is a perfect pairing.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The pairing is well defined: changing $c$ by an element of
$\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}$ or $x$ by an element of $\mathfrak p_E^q$ changes $cx/\Gamma$ by
an element of $\mathfrak p_E^{-n}$, on which $\psi$ is trivial.  The annihilator
of $\mathfrak p_E^r/\mathfrak p_E^q$ in the first factor is zero, because
\[
 c\mathfrak p_E^r/\Gamma\subseteq\mathfrak p_E^{-n}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 c\in\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}.
\]
Similarly, the annihilator of the first factor in the second is zero,
because
\[
 \mathfrak p_E^{M-q}x/\Gamma\subseteq\mathfrak p_E^{-n}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x\in\mathfrak p_E^q.
\]
Thus the pairing is nondegenerate in both variables.  Both finite
additive groups have cardinality $q_E^{q-r}$, hence the induced maps to
the respective character groups are isomorphisms.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:stationary-class-existence}
Let $q=m_E(\theta)>1$, let $n=n_E(\psi)$, choose an integer $M$ and
an element $\Gamma\in E^\times$ such that
\[
 \Gamma\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^{M+n},
\]
and let $r$ satisfy
\[
 \left\lceil q/2\right\rceil\le r\le q-1.
\]
There is a unique class
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{St}_{\Gamma,r}(\theta)
 \in \mathfrak p_E^{M-q}/\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}
\end{equation*}
such that every representative $c$ of this class satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-stationary-linearization}
 \theta(1+x)=\psi(cx/\Gamma)
 \qquad(x\in\mathfrak p_E^r).
\end{equation}
Every representative $c$ has exact valuation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-stationary-valuation}
 v_E(c)=M-q.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For $x,y\in\mathfrak p_E^r$, the quotient
\[
 \frac{(1+x)(1+y)}{1+x+y}
 =1+\frac{xy}{1+x+y}
\]
belongs to $U_E^q$, because $2r\ge q$.  Hence
$x\mapsto\theta(1+x)$ is an additive character of
$\mathfrak p_E^r/\mathfrak p_E^q$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-duality}, applied with the
present $M,q,r,\Gamma$, identifies the character group of
$\mathfrak p_E^r/\mathfrak p_E^q$ with
$\mathfrak p_E^{M-q}/\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}$.  This gives the unique class
in the statement satisfying
\eqref{eq:general-stationary-linearization}.

Every representative belongs to $\mathfrak p_E^{M-q}$.  If it belonged to
$\mathfrak p_E^{M-q+1}$, then for every $x\in\mathfrak p_E^{q-1}$ one would have
$cx/\Gamma\in\mathfrak p_E^{-n}$.  Since $r\le q-1$, such $x$ lies in the
linearization domain, and
\eqref{eq:general-stationary-linearization} would make $\theta$ trivial
on $U_E^{q-1}$, contrary to the exact conductor $q$.  Thus
$v_E(c)=M-q$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:stationary-class-calculus}
Use the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:stationary-class-existence}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $r\le s\le q-1$, restriction from $\mathfrak p_E^r$ to $\mathfrak p_E^s$
      sends $\operatorname{St}_{\Gamma,r}(\theta)$ to the class of the
      same representative modulo $\mathfrak p_E^{M-s}$.
\item If $\Gamma'=a\Gamma$, then $ac$ represents the stationary class
      relative to $\Gamma'$ whenever $c$ represents the class relative
      to $\Gamma$.
\item Let $\theta_1,\theta_2$ be characters and suppose that, on a
      common depth $r$, coefficients $c_1,c_2$ satisfy
      \[
       \theta_i(1+x)=\psi(c_ix/\Gamma)\qquad(x\in\mathfrak p_E^r).
      \]
      Then $c_1+c_2$ represents the restriction of
      $\theta_1\theta_2$ on that depth, and $jc_1$ represents the
      restriction of the integer power $\theta_1^j$.  These assertions
      are equalities of classes modulo $\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}$.
\item Suppose $m_E(\theta_1)=m_E(\theta_2)=q$, take
      $\left\lceil q/2\right\rceil\le r\le q-1$, and choose representatives
      $c_i$ of $\operatorname{St}_{\Gamma,r}(\theta_i)$ for $i=1,2$.
      Then
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:stationary-leading-cancellation}
       m_E(\theta_1\theta_2)<q
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       c_1+c_2\in\mathfrak p_E^{M-q+1}.
      \end{equation}
      If $1<q'=m_E(\theta_1\theta_2)<q$, put
      $r'=\left\lceil q'/2\right\rceil$ and choose a representative
      $c'$ of $\operatorname{St}_{\Gamma,r'}(\theta_1\theta_2)$.  Then
      \[
       c'\equiv c_1+c_2\pmod{\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}}.
      \]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Parts (a) and (b) follow immediately from
\eqref{eq:general-stationary-linearization} and uniqueness.  Part (c)
follows by multiplying the two character identities; uniqueness at the
common depth identifies the resulting class modulo $\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}$.

For (d), the product has conductor less than $q$ precisely when it is
trivial on $U_E^{q-1}$.  For $x\in\mathfrak p_E^{q-1}$, part (c) gives
\[
 (\theta_1\theta_2)(1+x)=\psi((c_1+c_2)x/\Gamma).
\]
The annihilator of $\mathfrak p_E^{q-1}$ is $\mathfrak p_E^{M-q+1}$, which proves
\eqref{eq:stationary-leading-cancellation}.

Now suppose $1<q'=m_E(\theta_1\theta_2)<q$.  Since $r'\le r$, the
linearization defining $c'$ is valid for every $x\in\mathfrak p_E^r$, and part
(c) gives the same character there using $c_1+c_2$.  Thus
\[
 \psi((c'-c_1-c_2)x/\Gamma)=1
 \qquad(x\in\mathfrak p_E^r).
\]
The annihilator of $\mathfrak p_E^r$ is $\mathfrak p_E^{M-r}$, proving the asserted
congruence.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-quadratic-magnitude}
Let $V$ be a finite abelian group and let $q:V\to\mathbf C^\times$ satisfy
$|q(x)|=1$, $q(0)=1$, and
\[
 B(x,y)=\frac{q(x+y)}{q(x)q(y)}.
\]
Assume that $B$ is a nondegenerate bicharacter.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-quadratic-magnitude}
 \left|\sum_{x\in V}q(x)\right|^2=|V|.
\end{equation}
In particular, the sum is nonzero.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Put $S=\sum_xq(x)$.  Since $\overline{q(y)}=q(y)^{-1}$, the change of
variables $x=y+h$ gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |S|^2
 &=\sum_{x,y\in V}q(x)\overline{q(y)}
   =\sum_{h,y\in V}q(y+h)q(y)^{-1}\\
 &=\sum_{h\in V}q(h)\sum_{y\in V}B(h,y).
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $h=0$ the inner sum is $|V|$.  For $h\ne0$, nondegeneracy says that
$B(h,\cdot)$ is a nontrivial character, whose sum is zero.  Hence only
$h=0$ survives and $|S|^2=|V|$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Lamprecht}
Put
\[
 \beta=\beta(\theta):=
 \operatorname{St}_{\gamma,d+\varepsilon}(\theta)
 \in\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak p_E^d.
\]
Equivalently, $\beta$ is the unique class satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lamprecht-linearization}
 \theta(1+x)=\psi(\beta x/\gamma)
 \qquad(x\in\mathfrak p_E^{d+\varepsilon}).
\end{equation}
Every representative of this class is a unit.  Fix any representative,
again denoted $\beta\in\mathcal O_E^\times$.  If $\varepsilon=0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lamprecht-even}
 \Delta_E(\theta,\psi)=
 \theta(\gamma)\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
If $\varepsilon=1$, choose $\delta\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^d$; we call
$\delta$ a \emph{critical element}.  Via
$\bar x\mapsto\delta x\pmod{\mathfrak p_E^{d+1}}$, identify $k_E$ with
$\mathfrak p_E^d/\mathfrak p_E^{d+1}$, the \emph{critical line}.  For
$\bar x\in k_E$, choose a lift $x\in\mathcal O_E$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function}
 H_E(\bar x)=
 \psi(\delta\beta x/\gamma)\theta(1+\delta x)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
We call $H_E$ the \emph{critical function}.  It is well defined and
unimodular, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lamprecht-odd}
 \Delta_E(\theta,\psi)=
 \theta(\gamma)\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}
 \operatorname{ph}\!\left(\sum_{x\in k_E}H_E(x)\right).
\end{equation}
The right side of \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-odd} is independent of the
choice of $\delta$ with $\delta\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^d$.  Moreover, for
$\bar x,\bar y\in k_E$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hasse-functional-equation}
 H_E(\bar x+\bar y)=
 H_E(\bar x)H_E(\bar y)\psi_0(\bar x\bar y),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lamprecht-residual-character}
 \psi_0(\bar z)=\psi(\beta\delta^2 z/\gamma),
 \qquad z\in\mathcal O_E\text{ a lift of }\bar z\in k_E,
\end{equation}
is a well-defined nontrivial additive character of $k_E$.  Consequently
\[
 \left|\sum_{x\in k_E}H_E(x)\right|=q_E^{1/2}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:stationary-class-existence} with
\[
 q=M=m=2d+\varepsilon,
 \qquad \Gamma=\gamma,
 \qquad r=d+\varepsilon.
\]
Since $M-q=0$ and $M-r=d$, it gives the class
$\beta\in\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak p_E^d$ characterized by
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-linearization};
\eqref{eq:general-stationary-valuation} gives $v_E(\beta)=0$ for every
representative.  This proves the first assertions of the theorem.

Put
\[
 I=\int_{U_E^0}\psi(u/\gamma)\theta(u)^{-1}\,du,
 \qquad A=\mathfrak p_E^{d+\varepsilon}/\mathfrak p_E^m.
\]
For each $x\in A$, substitute $u\mapsto u(1+x)$ in the integral.  Haar
measure on $U_E^0$ is translation invariant, and
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-linearization} gives
\[
 I=\int_{U_E^0}\psi(u/\gamma)\theta(u)^{-1}
       \psi((u-\beta)x/\gamma)\,du.
\]
Average this identity over $x\in A$.  Character orthogonality and
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-duality}, specialized to
$M=q=m$, $r=d+\varepsilon$, and $\Gamma=\gamma$, give
\begin{equation*}
 \frac1{|A|}\sum_{x\in A}\psi((u-\beta)x/\gamma)
 =\begin{cases}
 1,&u-\beta\in\mathfrak p_E^d,\\
 0,&u-\beta\notin\mathfrak p_E^d.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Hence only the compact open subset
$\beta(1+\mathfrak p_E^d)$ survives.

Assume first that $m=2d$.  Write $u=\beta(1+z)$ with
$z\in\mathfrak p_E^d$.  The linearization identity gives
$\theta(1+z)=\psi(\beta z/\gamma)$.  Therefore on the surviving set
\[
 \psi(u/\gamma)\theta(u)^{-1}
 =\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}.
\]
The integral is this nonzero constant times the positive measure of the
surviving set.  Taking its phase proves \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-even}.

Now assume that $m=2d+1$.  Since $m>1$, one has $d\ge1$.  Partition
$\beta(1+\mathfrak p_E^d)$ into its $q_E$ cosets of
$1+\mathfrak p_E^{d+1}$.  They are represented by
$u_x=\beta(1+\delta x)$, where $x\in\mathcal O_E$ is a lift of $\bar x\in k_E$.  If
$w\in\mathfrak p_E^{d+1}$, then the quotient of the integrand at
$u_x(1+w)$ by its value at $u_x$ is
\[
 \psi(u_xw/\gamma)\theta(1+w)^{-1}.
\]
Linearization gives $\theta(1+w)=\psi(\beta w/\gamma)$, while
$(u_x-\beta)w\in\mathfrak p_E^{2d+1}=\mathfrak p_E^m$; hence the displayed quotient is
one.  Thus the integrand is constant on each of the $q_E$ cosets.  In
particular, changing the lift $x$ of $\bar x$ does not change the value
of $H_E(\bar x)$, so $H_E$ is well defined.  It is
unimodular because $|\psi(\delta\beta x/\gamma)|=1$ and the
restriction of the quasi-character $\theta$ to the compact group
$U_E^0$ has values of absolute value one.  The value of the integrand
at $u_x$ is
\[
 \psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}H_E(\bar x).
\]
As in the even case, integrating a constant over each coset contributes
its value times the common positive Haar measure
$c=\operatorname{vol}(1+\mathfrak p_E^{d+1})$.  Hence
\[
 I=c\,\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}
      \sum_{\bar x\in k_E}H_E(\bar x).
\]
Since $I\ne0$, one has $\sum_{\bar x\in k_E}H_E(\bar x)\ne0$.  Taking phases therefore
gives \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-odd}.  If $\delta'=v\delta$ with $v\in\mathcal O_E^\times$, and
$H_E'$ is formed using $\delta'$, then
\[
 H_E'(\bar x)=H_E(\bar v\,\bar x),
\]
because $vx$ is a lift of $\bar v\,\bar x$.  Multiplication by
$\bar v\in k_E^\times$ permutes $k_E$, so
$\sum_{\bar x}H_E'(\bar x)=
 \sum_{\bar x}H_E(\bar x)$.  This proves the asserted
independence of $\delta$.

For $\bar x,\bar y\in k_E$, choose lifts $x,y\in\mathcal O_E$ and put
\[
 w=\frac{\delta^2xy}{1+\delta(x+y)}.
\]
Then
\[
 (1+\delta x)(1+\delta y)=(1+\delta(x+y))(1+w).
\]
The additive linear factors in \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function}
cancel, so
\[
 \frac{H_E(\bar x+\bar y)}
      {H_E(\bar x)H_E(\bar y)}
 =\theta(1+w)=\psi(\beta w/\gamma).
\]
Since $w-\delta^2xy\in\mathfrak p_E^{3d}$ and
$3d\ge2d+1=m$, the last expression equals
$\psi(\beta\delta^2xy/\gamma)$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:Hasse-functional-equation} and
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-residual-character}.  Put
$a=\beta\delta^2/\gamma$.  Since
$v_E(a)=-n_E(\psi)-1$, changing a lift $z$ of $\bar z$ by an element
of $\mathfrak p_E$ changes $az$ by an element of $\mathfrak p_E^{-n_E(\psi)}$, on
which $\psi$ is trivial.  Hence $\psi_0$ is well defined.  If
$\psi_0$ were trivial, then $\psi$ would be trivial on
$a\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^{-n_E(\psi)-1}$, contradicting the definition of
$n_E(\psi)$.  Thus $\psi_0$ is nontrivial.  The bicharacter
$(x,y)\mapsto\psi_0(xy)$ is nondegenerate: for $x\ne0$, multiplication
by $x$ is a bijection of $k_E$, so $y\mapsto\psi_0(xy)$ is nontrivial.
Equation~\eqref{eq:finite-quadratic-magnitude} now gives
$\left|\sum_{x\in k_E}H_E(x)\right|=q_E^{1/2}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:complete-stationary-invariant}
The stationary expression in Lamprecht's formula is independent
of the representative of the class
$\beta\in\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak p_E^d$.  More precisely, if
$\beta'=\beta+h$ with $h\in\mathfrak p_E^d$, then the right sides of
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-even} and \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-odd}, respectively,
are unchanged when $\beta$ is replaced by $\beta'$ and the Hasse
function \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function} is formed with $\beta'$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Suppose first that $m=2d$.  Since $\beta$ is a unit,
$z=h/\beta$ lies in $\mathfrak p_E^d$, and the linearization formula gives
$\theta(1+z)=\psi(\beta z/\gamma)=\psi(h/\gamma)$.  Hence
\[
 \frac{\psi(\beta'/\gamma)\theta(\beta')^{-1}}
      {\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}}
 =\psi(h/\gamma)\theta(1+h/\beta)^{-1}=1.
\]

Now let $m=2d+1$.  Choose $\delta\mathcal O_E=\mathfrak p_E^d$ and write
\[
 a=\frac{h}{\beta\delta}\in\mathcal O_E,
 \qquad \bar a\in k_E
\]
for its residue class.  Let $H_\beta$ and $H_{\beta'}$ denote the
Hasse functions formed with $\beta$ and $\beta'$.  For
$\bar x\in k_E$, choose a lift $x\in\mathcal O_E$.  Directly from
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function},
\begin{equation*}
 H_{\beta'}(\bar x)
 =H_\beta(\bar x)\,\psi(\delta h x/\gamma).
\end{equation*}
The functional equation \eqref{eq:Hasse-functional-equation} gives
\[
 H_\beta(\bar x+\bar a)
 =H_\beta(\bar x)H_\beta(\bar a)
   \psi(\beta\delta^2ax/\gamma).
\]
Since $\beta\delta a=h$, one has
$\psi(\beta\delta^2ax/\gamma)=\psi(\delta hx/\gamma)$.  Therefore
\[
 H_{\beta'}(\bar x)
 =H_\beta(\bar a)^{-1}H_\beta(\bar x+\bar a),
 \qquad
 \sum_{\bar x\in k_E}H_{\beta'}(\bar x)
 =H_\beta(\bar a)^{-1}\sum_{\bar x\in k_E}H_\beta(\bar x).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 \frac{\psi(\beta'/\gamma)\theta(\beta')^{-1}}
      {\psi(\beta/\gamma)\theta(\beta)^{-1}}
 =\psi(h/\gamma)\theta(1+\delta a)^{-1}
 =H_\beta(\bar a).
\]
Because the Hasse sums are nonzero, taking phases shows that these two
multipliers cancel.  Thus the odd-conductor stationary factor
is also unchanged.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:stable-twist-new}
Let $\nu$ be a quasi-character of $E^\times$.  If
$m_E(\theta)=2d+\varepsilon>1$ and $m_E(\nu)\leq d$, then, for any
representative $\beta$ of the stationary class of $\theta$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-twist-new}
 \Delta_E(\nu\theta,\psi)=
 \nu(\gamma/\beta)\Delta_E(\theta,\psi).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Since $m_E(\nu)\le d<m$, the character $\nu$ is trivial on
$U_E^{m-1}$.  Thus $\nu\theta$ is nontrivial on
$U_E^{m-1}$ and trivial on $U_E^m$, so
\[
 m_E(\nu\theta)=m_E(\theta)=m.
\]
Moreover, $\nu$ is trivial on $U_E^d$, hence on
$U_E^{d+\varepsilon}$.  Therefore $\theta$ and $\nu\theta$ have the
same restriction to the stationary layer $U_E^{d+\varepsilon}$, so
their stationary classes coincide.  Choose the same representative
$\beta$ for both.  If $m$ is even, both residual factors are $1$;
if $m$ is odd, their Hasse functions are identical.  Taking the ratio in
\eqref{eq:Delta-factorization-new} gives
$\nu(\gamma)\nu(\beta)^{-1}$, proving
\eqref{eq:stable-twist-new}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:minimal-orbit-stationary}
Let $K/F$ be ramified cyclic of prime degree $\ell$, let $t$ be its
break, put $T=t+1$, and let $\tau$ be a nontrivial element of
$S(K/F)$.  Retain the minimal-conductor choice of $\chi_F$.
Put $m=m_F(\chi_F)$.  Then, for every nontrivial
power $\tau^j$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:minimal-orbit-conductors}
 m_F(\tau^j\chi_F)=\max\{m,T\}.
\end{equation}
If $T>1$ and $m=T$, choose $\Gamma$ with
\[
 \Gamma\mathcal O_F=\mathfrak p_F^{m+n_F(\psi_F)},
\]
choose
\[
 \left\lceil m/2\right\rceil\le r\le m-1,
\]
and choose $a,b\in\mathcal O_F^\times$ such that
\[
 \tau(1+x)=\psi_F(ax/\Gamma),
 \qquad
 \chi_F(1+x)=\psi_F(bx/\Gamma)
 \qquad(x\in\mathfrak p_F^r).
\]
Then, for $j=0,\ldots,\ell-1$, viewed as integers in $F$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:minimal-orbit-no-leading-cancellation}
 b+ja\notin\mathfrak p_F.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
A nontrivial norm character has conductor $T$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:norm-characters}.  If $m<T$, then $\chi_F$ is trivial
on $U_F^{T-1}$, whereas $\tau^j$ is not, so the product has conductor
$T$.  If $m>T$, then $\tau^j$ is trivial on $U_F^{m-1}$, whereas
$\chi_F$ is not, so the product has conductor $m$.  If $m=T$, every
member of the orbit has conductor at least $T$ by minimality of $\chi_F$ in its orbit, and at most $T$ because both factors are trivial on $U_F^T$.
This proves \eqref{eq:minimal-orbit-conductors}.

Assume $T>1$ and $m=T$.  For $x\in\mathfrak p_F^r$, the two displayed
linearizations give
\[
 (\tau^j\chi_F)(1+x)=\psi_F((b+ja)x/\Gamma).
\]
If $b+ja\in\mathfrak p_F$, equation
\eqref{eq:stationary-leading-cancellation}, with $M=q=m$, would give
conductor less than $m$, contradicting
\eqref{eq:minimal-orbit-conductors}.  This proves
\eqref{eq:minimal-orbit-no-leading-cancellation}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-gauss-magnitude}
For
\[
 G_k(\chi,\psi)=\sum_{x\in k^\times}\chi(x)\psi(x)
\]
one has $G_k(1,\psi)=-1$.  If $\chi$ is nontrivial, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-gauss-magnitude}
 |G_k(\chi,\psi)|^2=|k|.
\end{equation}
Consequently every $G_k(\chi,\psi)$ and every
$\tau_k(\chi,\psi)$ is nonzero.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The trivial-character formula is
$\sum_{x\in k^\times}\psi(x)=-1$, because the sum over all of $k$ is
zero.  Assume $\chi$ nontrivial and write $q=|k|$.  Since the values of
$\chi$ and $\psi$ have absolute value one,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |G_k(\chi,\psi)|^2
 &=\sum_{x,y\in k^\times}\chi(x/y)\psi(x-y)\\
 &=\sum_{t\in k^\times}\chi(t)
       \sum_{y\in k^\times}\psi((t-1)y).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The inner sum is $q-1$ when $t=1$ and is $-1$ when $t\ne1$.
Therefore
\[
 |G_k(\chi,\psi)|^2
 =(q-1)-\sum_{t\ne1}\chi(t).
\]
Character orthogonality gives $\sum_{t\in k^\times}\chi(t)=0$, so
$\sum_{t\ne1}\chi(t)=-1$ and the last expression is $q$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:HD-lift}
For a finite extension $k'/k$ of degree $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HD-lift}
 \tau_{k'}(\chi\circ N_{k'/k},\psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{k'/k})
 =\tau_k(\chi,\psi)^f.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
This is the classical lifting relation of Davenport and Hasse
\cite{DavenportHasse}.  We include the Euler-product proof in the
normalization used here.


For a monic polynomial
\[
 P(X)=X^r+a_1X^{r-1}+\cdots+a_r\in k[X],\qquad a_r\ne0,
\]
put
\[
 w(P)=\chi((-1)^r a_r)\psi(-a_1).
\]
If $P,Q$ are monic with nonzero constant terms, then the constant terms
multiply and the negative of the coefficient of degree
$\deg(PQ)-1$ is the sum of the roots; hence $w(PQ)=w(P)w(Q)$.  Therefore
\begin{align*}
 L(T)
 &=\prod_{\substack{P\ {\rm monic\ irreducible}\\ P\ne X}}
       (1-w(P)T^{\deg P})^{-1}\\
 &=\sum_{\substack{P\ {\rm monic}\\ P(0)\ne0}}w(P)T^{\deg P}.
\end{align*}
For degree $r\ge2$, the coefficient is zero, because $a_1$ ranges freely
through $k$ and $\sum_{a_1\in k}\psi(-a_1)=0$.  The coefficient in
degree $1$ is
\[
 \sum_{a_1\ne0}\chi(-a_1)\psi(-a_1)=G_k(\chi,\psi).
\]
Thus
\begin{equation*}
 L(T)=1+G_k(\chi,\psi)T.
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, taking logarithms of the Euler product and grouping
closed points after extension of scalars gives
\begin{equation*}
 \log L(T)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{T^r}{r}
 \sum_{x\in k_r^\times}
     \chi(N_{k_r/k}x)\psi(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k}x),
\end{equation*}
where $k_r/k$ is the degree-$r$ extension.  Indeed, an element of $k_r$
of degree $d\mid r$ contributes through its monic minimal polynomial
with multiplicity $d$, as in the usual Euler-product proof for
the zeta function of the affine line.  Comparing the displayed formulas for $L(T)$ and $\log L(T)$ yields
\begin{equation*}
 G_{k_r}(\chi\circ N_{k_r/k},\psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k})
 =(-1)^{r-1}G_k(\chi,\psi)^r.
\end{equation*}
Now apply this identity to $\chi^{-1}$.  Since
$\tau_k(\chi,\psi)=-G_k(\chi^{-1},\psi)$, the signs cancel:
\[
 \tau_{k_r}(\chi\circ N_{k_r/k},\psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k})
 =-(-1)^{r-1}G_k(\chi^{-1},\psi)^r
 =\tau_k(\chi,\psi)^r.
\]
Taking $r=f$ proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:HD-product}
Let $\ell\mid |k^\times|$, let
$\eta:k^\times\to\mathbf C^\times$ be a multiplicative character of order
$\ell$, and let $\chi:k^\times\to\mathbf C^\times$ be any multiplicative
character.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HD-product}
 \chi(\ell^\ell)\tau_k(\chi^\ell,\psi)
 \prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\tau_k(\eta^j,\psi)
 =\tau_k(\chi,\psi)
 \prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\tau_k(\chi\eta^j,\psi).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
For
\[
 G(\alpha)=\sum_{x\in k^\times}\alpha(x)\psi(x),
 \qquad G(1)=-1,
\]
the classical Davenport--Hasse multiplication formula
\cite{DavenportHasse} is
\[
 \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}G(\alpha\eta^j)
 =\alpha(\ell^{-\ell})G(\alpha^\ell)
   \prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1}G(\eta^j).
\]
Apply it with $\alpha=\chi^{-1}$.  Inversion permutes the nontrivial powers of
$\eta$, and $G(\alpha)=-\tau_k(\alpha^{-1},\psi)$.  Both sides contain
exactly $\ell$ ordinary Gauss sums when the factor
$G(\chi^{-\ell})$ is counted, so the signs cancel.  Finally
$\chi^{-1}(\ell^{-\ell})=\chi(\ell^\ell)$, which gives
\eqref{eq:HD-product} in Langlands's normalization.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hasse-lift}
Let $k'/k$ be finite and let a nowhere-zero function $H:k\to\mathbf C^\times$
satisfy
\[
 H(x+y)=H(x)H(y)\psi(xy).
\]
Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hasse-lift-definition}
 \omega_{k'/k}(x)=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}}x^\sigma x^\tau,
 \qquad
 H_{k'/k}(x)=
 H(\operatorname{Tr} x)\psi(-\omega_{k'/k}(x)).
\end{equation}
Here the sum defining $\omega_{k'/k}$ is over the unordered pairs of
distinct $k$-embeddings $k'\hookrightarrow\overline{k}$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hasse-lift-sum}
 -\sum_{x\in k'}H_{k'/k}(x)
 =\left(-\sum_{x\in k}H(x)\right)^{[k':k]}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
For the sum identity, let
\[
 P(X)=X^r+a_1X^{r-1}+a_2X^{r-2}+\cdots
\]
be monic and put
\[
 w(P)=H(-a_1)\psi(-a_2),
\]
where $a_2=0$ in degree $1$.  If $Q$ has first coefficients $b_1,b_2$,
then the first two coefficients of $PQ$ are
$a_1+b_1$ and $a_2+b_2+a_1b_1$.  Hence
\begin{align*}
 w(PQ)
 &=H(-a_1-b_1)\psi(-a_2-b_2-a_1b_1)\\
 &=H(-a_1)H(-b_1)\psi(a_1b_1)
   \psi(-a_2-b_2-a_1b_1)=w(P)w(Q).
\end{align*}
Thus
\[
 L(T)=\prod_{P\ {\rm monic\ irreducible}}
       (1-w(P)T^{\deg P})^{-1}
     =\sum_{P\ {\rm monic}}w(P)T^{\deg P}.
\]
For degree $r\ge2$, the coefficient is zero because $a_2$ ranges freely
and $\psi$ is nontrivial.  In degree $1$ it is $\sum_{x\in k}H(x)$.
Therefore
\begin{equation*}
 L(T)=1+\left(\sum_{x\in k}H(x)\right)T.
\end{equation*}
We next justify the closed-point expansion, including compatibility
with repeated closed points.  Let $P$ be monic irreducible of degree
$d$, choose a root $\xi\in k_d$, and put
\[
 s=\operatorname{Tr}_{k_d/k}(\xi),\qquad e=\omega_{k_d/k}(\xi).
\]
The first two coefficients of $P$ are $-s$ and $e$, so
\[
 w(P)=H(s)\psi(-e).
\]
If $r=hd$ and $\xi$ is viewed in $k_r$, each of its $d$ conjugates
occurs $h$ times.  Consequently
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k}(\xi)=hs,
 \qquad
 \omega_{k_r/k}(\xi)=he+\binom h2s^2.
\end{equation*}
Iteration of the functional equation for $H$ gives
\begin{equation*}
 H(hs)=H(s)^h\psi\!\left(\binom h2s^2\right).
\end{equation*}
Combining these identities yields
\begin{equation*}
 H(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k}\xi)\psi(-\omega_{k_r/k}(\xi))
 =\bigl(H(s)\psi(-e)\bigr)^h=w(P)^h.
\end{equation*}
By this identity, the $d$ roots belonging
to the closed point $P$ contribute
$d\,w(P)^h$ to the sum over $k_r$.  Expanding the logarithm of the
Euler product and regrouping by $r=h\deg P$ therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
 \log L(T)
 =\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{T^r}{r}
 \sum_{x\in k_r}H(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_r/k}x)
              \psi(-\omega_{k_r/k}(x)).
\end{equation*}
Comparing the logarithm of the linear formula for $L(T)$ with
this expansion gives
\[
 \sum_{x\in k_r}H_{k_r/k}(x)
 =(-1)^{r-1}\left(\sum_{x\in k}H(x)\right)^r.
\]
Multiplying by $-1$ gives \eqref{eq:Hasse-lift-sum}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:quadratic-phase-new}
Assume $\operatorname{char}k\neq2$.  Define the quadratic
character
$\nu:k^\times\to\{\pm1\}$ by
\[
 \nu(a)=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&a\in(k^\times)^2,\\
  -1,&a\notin(k^\times)^2,
 \end{cases}
\]
and extend it by $\nu(0)=0$.  Put
\[
 Q_\psi(a,b)=\operatorname{ph}\!\left(\sum_{x\in k}
     \psi\left(\frac a2x^2+bx\right)\right),\qquad a\neq0.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-phase-new}
 Q_\psi(a,b)=\nu(a)\psi(-b^2/2a)Q_\psi(1,0),
 \qquad Q_\psi(1,0)^2=\nu(-1).
\end{equation}
The defining sum has absolute value $|k|^{1/2}$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let
\[
 S(a,b)=\sum_{x\in k}\psi\left(\frac a2x^2+bx\right).
\]
Completing the square gives
\[
 S(a,b)=\psi(-b^2/2a)S(a,0).
\]
For $c\ne0$, every $y\in k^\times$ has $1+\nu(y)$ square roots, while
zero has one square root.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-gauss-rescaling}
 \sum_{x\in k}\psi(cx^2)
 =\sum_{y\in k^\times}\nu(y)\psi(cy)
 =\nu(c)G_k(\nu,\psi).
\end{equation}
The additive-character part disappeared because
$\sum_{y\in k}\psi(cy)=0$.  Taking $c=a/2$ in \eqref{eq:quadratic-gauss-rescaling} and comparing with $a=1$
proves the first phase identity.  Equation~\eqref{eq:finite-gauss-magnitude}
shows at once that $|S(a,b)|=|k|^{1/2}$.

It remains to compute the square of the phase.  Put
$G=G_k(\nu,\psi)$.  Changing variables $x=ty$ in the product of the
two Gauss sums gives
\[
 G^2=\sum_{t\in k^\times}\nu(t)
       \sum_{y\in k^\times}\psi((t+1)y).
\]
Here the inner sum is $|k|-1$ for $t=-1$ and is $-1$ for
$t\ne-1$.  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 G^2
 &=\nu(-1)(|k|-1)-\sum_{t\ne-1}\nu(t)\\
 &=\nu(-1)(|k|-1)+\nu(-1)
  =\nu(-1)|k|,
 \end{aligned}
\]
because $\sum_{t\in k^\times}\nu(t)=0$.  Since
$S(1,0)=\nu(1/2)G$ and $\nu(1/2)^2=1$, dividing by absolute values
gives $Q_\psi(1,0)^2=\nu(-1)$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:ramified-Hasse-comparison}
Let $K/F$ be totally ramified cyclic of odd prime degree $\ell$, with
single break $t$.  Let $\chi_F:F^\times\to\mathbf C^\times$ be a
quasi-character and let $\psi_F:F\to\mathbf C^\times$ be a nontrivial additive
character.  Put
\[
 \chi_K=\chi_F\circ N_{K/F},
 \qquad
 \psi_K=\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}.
\]
Suppose
\[
 m_F(\chi_F)=2d+1>1,
\]
and assume either
\[
 t=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad d\ge t+1.
\]
Let $\Gamma\in F^\times$ be admissible for $(\chi_F,\psi_F)$, and let
$\beta\in\mathcal O_F^\times$ represent the stationary class of $\chi_F$
relative to $\Gamma$.  Then $\Gamma$ is also admissible for
$(\chi_K,\psi_K)$, and $\beta$ represents its stationary class.
With this common denominator and representative, the residual factors
satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramified-Hasse-comparison}
 \Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)=\Delta_{3,F}(\chi_F)^\ell.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-conductor}(i),
\[
 m_K(\chi_K)=\ell(2d+1)-(\ell-1)(t+1)=2d'+1,
 \qquad
 d'=\ell d-\frac{\ell-1}{2}t.
\]
Put $n=n_F(\psi_F)$ and choose uniformizers with
$\varpi_F=N(\varpi_K)$.  If $t>0$, choose a generator $\sigma$ of $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$
and define $\lambda$ by \eqref{eq:critical-ramification-coordinate}.
The different exponent is
$(\ell-1)(t+1)$, and therefore
\[
 n_K(\psi_K)=\ell n+(\ell-1)(t+1),
 \qquad
 (2d'+1)+n_K(\psi_K)=\ell(2d+1+n).
\]
Since $v_K(\Gamma)=\ell(2d+1+n)$, the denominator $\Gamma$ is also
admissible for $\chi_K$.
For $y\in\mathfrak p_K^{d'+1}$, \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} gives
$\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)\in\mathfrak p_F^{d+1}$, and the norm expansion gives
\[
 N(1+y)\equiv1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{2d+1}}.
\]
Indeed, if $t=0$, then $d'=\ell d$ and every degree-$j$ term with
$j\ge2$ has valuation at least $\lceil j(d'+1)/\ell\rceil\ge2d+1$.
If $t>0$, then $\ell=p$, and \eqref{eq:symmetric-bound} gives this
bound for $2\le j<p$, since
$2(d'+1)+(p-1)(t+1)=p(2d+1)+1$; the norm term has valuation at least
$d'+1\ge2d+1$ by \eqref{eq:symmetric-bound-last}.
The chosen representative $\beta$ therefore satisfies
\[
 \chi_K(1+y)=\chi_F(1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y))
 =\psi_F(\beta\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)/\Gamma)
 =\psi_K(\beta y/\Gamma)
 \qquad(y\in\mathfrak p_K^{d'+1}).
\]
Let $k$ be the common residue field and, for $x\in k$, choose a
lift $\widetilde x\in\mathcal O_F\subset\mathcal O_K$; use the same notation for
lifts of other elements of $k$.  Write $E_2(y)$ for the second
elementary symmetric function of the conjugates of $y$.  The critical function for $\chi_F$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramified-Hasse-F-function}
 H_F(x)=
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{\beta\varpi_F^d\widetilde x}{\Gamma}\right)
 \chi_F(1+\varpi_F^d\widetilde x)^{-1},
\end{equation}
and its polar character is
\[
 \psi_0(z)=
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{\beta\varpi_F^{2d}\widetilde z}{\Gamma}\right).
\]
Put $Y=\varpi_K^{d'}\widetilde x$.  We claim that the critical function for $\chi_K$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramified-Hasse-K-function}
 H_K(x)=
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{\beta\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(Y)}{\Gamma}\right)
 \chi_F\!\left(1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(Y)+E_2(Y)\right)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, it is enough to prove
\begin{equation*}
 N(1+Y)
 \equiv1+\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(Y)+E_2(Y)
       \pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{2d+1}}.
\end{equation*}
If $t=0$, then $d'=\ell d$.  Every term of degree at least three in
the norm has valuation at least $3d\ge2d+1$, and the norm term has
valuation at least $\ell d\ge2d+1$.  If $t>0$, then $\ell=p$ is the residue
characteristic and $d\ge t+1$.  For $3\le j\le p-1$,
Equation~\eqref{eq:symmetric-bound} gives
\[
 v_F(s_j(Y))\ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{j d'+(p-1)(t+1)}p\right\rfloor
 \ge2d+1,
\]
while
\[
 v_F(NY)\ge d'=pd-\frac{p-1}{2}t\ge2d+1.
\]
This proves the claimed norm congruence.
Theorem~\ref{thm:Lamprecht} gives the independence of the lift in
\eqref{eq:ramified-Hasse-K-function}.  The same estimates also give
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(Y)\in\mathfrak p_F^d,
 \qquad E_2(Y)\in\mathfrak p_F^{2d},
\]
and one extra power of $\mathfrak p_F$ when $\widetilde x\in\mathfrak p_K$.

Set
\begin{equation*}
 \epsilon=
 \frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^{2d'})}{\varpi_F^{2d}}\in\mathcal O_F.
\end{equation*}
The preceding valuation estimates show that this quotient is integral.
We now show that it is a unit and determine its residue.  If $t=0$,
then
\[
 c=\overline{\varpi_K^{d'}/\varpi_F^d}\in k^\times
\]
is fixed by $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$, because $d'=\ell d$.  Hence
\begin{equation*}
 \bar\epsilon=\ell c^2.
\end{equation*}
If $t>0$, equation~\eqref{eq:stable-critical-trace-residue} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramified-epsilon-wild}
 \bar\epsilon=-\lambda^{p-1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\epsilon$ is a unit in both cases.

The functional equation \eqref{eq:Hasse-functional-equation} over $K$
gives directly
\begin{align*}
 \frac{H_K(x+y)}{H_K(x)H_K(y)}
 &=\psi_K\!\left(
   \frac{\beta\varpi_K^{2d'}\widetilde x\widetilde y}{\Gamma}\right)\\
 &=\psi_0(\bar\epsilon xy),
 \qquad x,y\in k,
\end{align*}
with $\epsilon=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\varpi_K^{2d'})/\varpi_F^{2d}$.  Since $\bar\epsilon\ne0$,
this polar bicharacter is nondegenerate.

We compare its normalized sum with that of $H_F$.  First assume that
$k$ has odd characteristic.  The polar character of $H_F$ is
$(x,y)\mapsto\psi_0(xy)$, so for a unique $\alpha_0\in k$ one has
\[
 H_F(x)=\psi_0(x^2/2+\alpha_0x).
\]
Put
\[
 T_x=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(Y)/\varpi_F^d},
 \qquad
 Q_x=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(Y^2)/\varpi_F^{2d}}.
\]
Using $\operatorname{Tr}(Y)/\varpi_F^d$ itself as a lift of $T_x$ in
\eqref{eq:ramified-Hasse-F-function}, one has
\[
 H_F(T_x)=
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{\beta\operatorname{Tr}(Y)}{\Gamma}\right)
 \chi_F(1+\operatorname{Tr}(Y))^{-1}.
\]
Because $E_2(Y)\in\mathfrak p_F^{2d}$,
\[
 \frac{1+\operatorname{Tr}(Y)}{1+\operatorname{Tr}(Y)+E_2(Y)}
 \equiv1-E_2(Y)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{2d+1}}.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-linearization}, applied to
$-E_2(Y)\in\mathfrak p_F^{2d}\subseteq\mathfrak p_F^{d+1}$, gives
\begin{equation*}
 H_K(x)=
 H_F(T_x)\,
 \psi_0\!\left(
  -\overline{\frac{E_2(Y)}{\varpi_F^{2d}}}\right).
\end{equation*}
Now
$2E_2(Y)=(\operatorname{Tr} Y)^2-\operatorname{Tr}(Y^2)$, so
\[
 -\overline{\frac{E_2(Y)}{\varpi_F^{2d}}}
 =\frac{Q_x-T_x^2}{2}.
\]
Substituting
$H_F(T_x)=\psi_0(T_x^2/2+\alpha_0T_x)$ in
$H_K(x)=H_F(T_x)\psi_0(-\overline{E_2(Y)/\varpi_F^{2d}})$ yields
\begin{equation*}
 H_K(x)=\psi_0(Q_x/2+\alpha_0T_x).
\end{equation*}
If $t=0$, substitute $T_x=\ell cx$ and $Q_x=\ell c^2x^2$ in
this expression for $H_K$ and replace $x$ by $c^{-1}x$:
\begin{equation*}
 H_K(c^{-1}x)=\psi_0(\ell x^2/2+\ell\alpha_0x).
\end{equation*}
Multiplication by $c^{-1}$ permutes $k$, so
$\sum_{x\in k}H_K(c^{-1}x)=\sum_{x\in k}H_K(x)$.
If $t>0$, the trace-ideal formula \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} gives $T_x=0$, while
$Q_x=\bar\epsilon x^2$, and hence
\begin{equation*}
 H_K(x)=\psi_0(\bar\epsilon x^2/2).
\end{equation*}
Let $\nu$ be the quadratic character of $k^\times$ and put
$Q=Q_{\psi_0}(1,0)$.  Suppose first that $t=0$.
Applying \eqref{eq:quadratic-phase-new} to the formula for
$H_K(c^{-1}x)$, the phase defining $\Delta_{3,F}(\chi_F)$ is
$Q\psi_0(-\alpha_0^2/2)$ and the phase defining
$\Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)$ is
\[
 \nu(\ell)Q\psi_0(-\ell\alpha_0^2/2).
\]
Since $Q^2=\nu(-1)$, the required power identity is equivalent to
\begin{equation*}
 \nu(\ell)=\nu(-1)^{(\ell-1)/2}.
\end{equation*}
Let $|k|=p^f$.  If $f$ is even, both sides are $1$.  If $f$ is odd,
the order of $p$ modulo $\ell$ is odd because $\ell\mid p^f-1$;
therefore $(p/\ell)=1$.  Quadratic reciprocity now gives
the required sign identity.

Now suppose $t>0$.  Then $\ell=p$ and
$\bar\epsilon=-\lambda^{p-1}$ by \eqref{eq:ramified-epsilon-wild}, so
$\nu(\bar\epsilon)=\nu(-1)$.  The formula for $H_K(x)$ in the case $t>0$ and $Q^2=\nu(-1)$ reduce the desired
identity to
\[
 \nu(-1)^{(p-3)/2}=1.
\]
If $p\equiv1\pmod4$, then $\nu(-1)=1$; if
$p\equiv3\pmod4$, the exponent $(p-3)/2$ is even.  This proves the
comparison in odd residue characteristic.

It remains to treat residue characteristic two.  Then $t=0$, because
$\ell$ is odd.  With $c=\overline{\varpi_K^{d'}/\varpi_F^d}$,
the norm calculation gives
\begin{equation*}
 H_K(c^{-1}x)
 =H_F(\ell x)\psi_0\!\left(-\binom{\ell}{2}x^2\right)
 =H_F(x)^\ell.
\end{equation*}
The second equality follows by iterating
$H_F(x+y)=H_F(x)H_F(y)\psi_0(xy)$.  Put
$S=\sum_x H_F(x)$ and $H=\operatorname{ph}(S)$.  Choose $c_0\in k^\times$ so
that $\psi_0(x^2)=\psi_0(c_0x)$.  Then
\[
 \overline{H_F(x)}=H_F(x)\psi_0(c_0x),
 \qquad
 \overline S=H_F(c_0)^{-1}S,
 \qquad
 H^2=H_F(c_0).
\]
As $H_F(x)^4=1$, the identity for $H_K(c^{-1}x)$ shows that the desired power
identity is equivalent to
\[
 H_F(c_0)^{(\ell-1)/2}=1\quad(\ell\equiv1\bmod4),
 \qquad
 H_F(c_0)^{(\ell+1)/2}=1\quad(\ell\equiv3\bmod4).
\]
Write $\psi_0(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}(a x)}$.  One may take
$c_0=a^{2^{f-1}-1}$, where $f=[k:\mathbf F_2]$; hence
\[
 H_F(c_0)^2=\psi_0(c_0^2)=(-1)^f.
\]
The two displayed powers are automatic for
$\ell\equiv1,7\pmod8$.  If $\ell\equiv3,5\pmod8$, then
$(2/\ell)=-1$; since $\ell\mid2^f-1$, the order of $2$ modulo
$\ell$ and therefore $f$ are even.  Thus $H_F(c_0)^2=1$, and the
remaining two residue classes also follow.

In every case the phase defining $\Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)$ is the
$\ell$th power of the phase defining $\Delta_{3,F}(\chi_F)$, which is
\eqref{eq:ramified-Hasse-comparison}.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:affine-pencil}
Let $k$ have odd characteristic $p$, normalize $\psi$ so that
$\psi(x^p)=\psi(x)$, take $\rho\in k^\times$ with
$1+j\rho\neq0$ for every $j\in\mathbf F_p$, and let $\sigma,\upsilon\in k$.
Choose $a_0,b_0\in k$ with
\[
 a_0^p=1-\rho^{1-p},\qquad
 b_0^p=\sigma-\rho^{-1}\upsilon.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 Q_\psi(a_0,b_0)
 \prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p^\times}Q_\psi(j\rho,j\upsilon)
 =\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p}Q_\psi(1+j\rho,\sigma+j\upsilon).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Apply \eqref{eq:quadratic-phase-new}.  The quadratic-character
parts agree because
\[
 \prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p}(1+j\rho)=1-\rho^{p-1},
 \qquad
 \prod_{j\neq0}j=-1,
\]
and $\nu(a_0)=\nu(1-\rho^{1-p})$.  The additive parts agree by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-sum}
 \sum_{j\in\mathbf F_p}\frac{(\sigma+j\upsilon)^2}{1+j\rho}
 =\frac{\rho^{p-3}(\sigma\rho-\upsilon)^2}{\rho^{p-1}-1}.
\end{equation}
To prove \eqref{eq:rational-sum}, use
\[
 \sum_j\frac1{1+j\rho}=\frac{\rho^{p-1}}{\rho^{p-1}-1},\quad
 \sum_j\frac{j}{1+j\rho}=-\frac{\rho^{p-2}}{\rho^{p-1}-1},\quad
 \sum_j\frac{j^2}{1+j\rho}=\frac{\rho^{p-3}}{\rho^{p-1}-1},
\]
which follow from the logarithmic derivative of
$\prod_j(X+j)=X^p-X$.  Finally the right side of
\eqref{eq:rational-sum} is $(b_0^2/a_0)^p$, and the normalization
$\psi(z^p)=\psi(z)$ finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:affine-pencil-homogeneous}
Under the hypotheses and notation of
Lemma~\ref{lem:affine-pencil}, let $c\in k^\times$.  Then
\begin{align*}
&\frac{
 Q_\psi(ca_0^p,cb_0^p)
 \displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p^\times}Q_\psi(cj\rho,cj\upsilon)}
 {\displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p}
 Q_\psi(c(1+j\rho),c(\sigma+j\upsilon))}
=
\frac{
 Q_\psi(a_0,b_0)
 \displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p^\times}Q_\psi(j\rho,j\upsilon)}
 {\displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathbf F_p}
 Q_\psi(1+j\rho,\sigma+j\upsilon)}.
\end{align*}
Thus a common nonzero scale  does not change the
normalized affine-pencil quotient.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For $a,c\ne0$, completion of the square gives
\[
 Q_\psi(ca,cb)
 =\nu(c)\psi\!\left(-\frac{(c-1)b^2}{2a}\right)Q_\psi(a,b),
\]
where $\nu$ is the quadratic character.  Apply this identity to every
factor of the quotient on the left.  The factors $\nu(c)$ cancel
because the numerator and denominator each contain $p$ factors.
The additive corrections cancel because
\[
 \frac{b_0^{2p}}{a_0^p}
 +\sum_{j\in\mathbf F_p^\times}\frac{(j\upsilon)^2}{j\rho}
 =\frac{b_0^{2p}}{a_0^p}
 =\sum_{j\in\mathbf F_p}\frac{(\sigma+j\upsilon)^2}{1+j\rho},
\]
using $\sum_{j\in\mathbf F_p^\times}j=0$ and
\eqref{eq:rational-sum}.  Finally,
$Q_\psi(a_0^p,b_0^p)=Q_\psi(a_0,b_0)$ by Frobenius invariance,
which gives the quotient on the right.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:AS-phase-new}
Let $k$ have characteristic $2$ and let
$\psi_0(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}(x)}$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:AS-phase}
 \psi_0(c+c^2)=1\qquad(c\in k).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The absolute trace is Frobenius-invariant, so
$\operatorname{Tr}(c+c^2)=0$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:stationary-depth-norm}
In each of the three cases above,
\begin{align}
 N_{K/F}(U_K^{d'+\varepsilon'})&\subseteq U_F^{d+\varepsilon},
                                                        \label{eq:stationary-depth-first-inclusion}\\
 N_{K/F}(U_K^{m'})&\subseteq U_F^m,             \label{eq:stationary-depth-second-inclusion}\\
 N_{K/F}(U_K^{d'})&\subseteq U_F^d.             \label{eq:stationary-parameter-ambiguity}
\end{align}
The third
inclusion implies that if $b,b'\in\mathcal O_K^\times$ and
$b'\equiv b\pmod{\mathfrak p_K^{d'}}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm-of-stationary-class-well-defined}
 N_{K/F}(b')\equiv N_{K/F}(b)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^d}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.
Put
\[
 q=\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil=d+\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 q'=\left\lceil\frac {m'}2\right\rceil=d'+\varepsilon'.
\]
In case (i), Lemma~\ref{lem:unramified-compatibility}(c) gives all
three inclusions.

Now consider case (ii), so $K/F$ is ramified and $m>t+1$.  We first
prove \eqref{eq:stationary-depth-first-inclusion}.  Set
$r=m-1>t$ and $s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor=q-1$.  Then
\[
 m'=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)+1,
 \qquad
 q'-1=\left\lfloor\frac{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
We claim that
\begin{equation*}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)}2\right\rfloor
 \ge \psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(s).
\end{equation*}
If $s\le t$, then the right side is $s$, whereas
$\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)\ge r\ge2s$.  If $s>t$, write
$r=2s+e$ with $e\in\{0,1\}$.  Equation~\eqref{eq:Herbrand-prime-new} gives
\[
 \psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(r)-2\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(s)
   =(\ell-1)t+\ell e\ge0,
\]
which again proves the claimed inequality.  Hence
\begin{equation*}
 q'\ge\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(q-1)+1.
\end{equation*}

If $q-1<t$, norm preserves the filtration below the break, so
$N(U_K^q)\subseteq U_F^q$.  If $q-1=t$, the critical norm map gives
$N(U_K^{t+1})\subseteq U_F^{t+1}$.  If $q-1>t$,
\eqref{eq:norm-above-break}, with $r=q-1$, gives
$N(U_K^{\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(q-1)+1})=U_F^q$.  Together with
the bound for $q'$ above and the decreasing unit
filtration, these three cases prove
\eqref{eq:stationary-depth-first-inclusion}.

For \eqref{eq:stationary-depth-second-inclusion},
\eqref{eq:norm-above-break}, applied with $r=m-1$, gives
$N(U_K^{m'})=U_F^m$.

We next prove \eqref{eq:stationary-parameter-ambiguity}.  Since
$\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(u)\ge u$, one has $m'\ge m$ and hence $d'\ge d$.  If
$d\le t$, norm preserves the filtration at depth $d$, so
\[
 N(U_K^{d'})\subseteq N(U_K^d)\subseteq U_F^d.
\]
If $d=t+1$, the same conclusion follows from the critical inclusion
$N(U_K^{t+1})\subseteq U_F^{t+1}$.  Finally suppose $d\ge t+2$ and put
\[
 R=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(d-1)+1.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:Herbrand-prime-new} and $m=2d+\varepsilon$, one obtains
\begin{align*}
 m'-2R
 &=\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(2d+\varepsilon-1)+1
     -2\bigl(\psi^{\mathrm H}_{K/F}(d-1)+1\bigr)\\
 &=(\ell-1)(t+1)+\ell\varepsilon\ge0.
\end{align*}
Thus $d'=\lfloor m'/2\rfloor\ge R$.  Equation
\eqref{eq:norm-above-break}, applied with $r=d-1$, now gives
\[
 N(U_K^{d'})\subseteq N(U_K^R)=U_F^d.
\]
This proves all three inclusions in case (ii).

Finally consider case (iii).  Here $m'=m\le t+1$, so $q'=q$ and
$d'=d\le t$.  Below the break, norm maps $U_K^i$ into $U_F^i$ for
every $i\le t$; at the last possible step $m=t+1$ one uses the
critical inclusion $N(U_K^{t+1})\subseteq U_F^{t+1}$.  Applying these
statements at $i=q$, $i=m$, and $i=d$ proves all three inclusions.

For the final assertion, write $b'=b(1+z)$ with
$z\in\mathfrak p_K^{d'}$.  Then $1+z\in U_K^{d'}$, so
\eqref{eq:stationary-parameter-ambiguity} gives
$N(b')/N(b)\in U_F^d$, which is equivalent to
\eqref{eq:norm-of-stationary-class-well-defined}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:truncated-norm-adjoint}
In each of cases (i)--(iii), the assignment
\[
 P_{K/F}(\bar y)=\overline{N_{K/F}(1+y)-1}
\]
is a well-defined additive homomorphism
\[
 P_{K/F}:\mathfrak p_K^{d'+\varepsilon'}/\mathfrak p_K^{m'}
 \longrightarrow\mathfrak p_F^{d+\varepsilon}/\mathfrak p_F^m.
\]
Let $\gamma_F$ and $\gamma_K$ be admissible denominators for
$(\chi_F,\psi_F)$ and $(\chi_K,\psi_K)$, respectively.  The pairings
\[
 (\bar x,\bar y)\longmapsto\psi_F(xy/\gamma_F),
 \qquad
 (\bar x',\bar y')\longmapsto\psi_K(x'y'/\gamma_K)
\]
between $\mathcal O_F/\mathfrak p_F^d$ and $\mathfrak p_F^{d+\varepsilon}/\mathfrak p_F^m$, and between
$\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p_K^{d'}$ and $\mathfrak p_K^{d'+\varepsilon'}/\mathfrak p_K^{m'}$, are perfect.
There is a unique additive adjoint
\[
 P^*_{K/F;\gamma_F,\gamma_K}:
 \mathcal O_F/\mathfrak p_F^d\longrightarrow\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p_K^{d'}
\]
with the following property: for $x\in\mathcal O_F$, an element $z\in\mathcal O_K$
represents $P^*_{K/F;\gamma_F,\gamma_K}(\bar x)$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pstar-def}
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{x(N_{K/F}(1+y)-1)}{\gamma_F}\right)
 =\psi_K(zy/\gamma_K)
 \qquad(y\in\mathfrak p_K^{d'+\varepsilon'}).
\end{equation}
If
\[
 N_{K/F}(1+y)-1\equiv\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^m}
 \qquad(y\in\mathfrak p_K^{d'+\varepsilon'})
\]
and $\gamma_K/\gamma_F\in\mathcal O_K^\times$, then
\[
 P^*_{K/F;\gamma_F,\gamma_K}(\bar x)
 =\overline{(\gamma_K/\gamma_F)x}
 \qquad(x\in\mathcal O_F).
\]
Under the same trace-congruence hypothesis, if $\gamma_K=\gamma_F$,
this is the map $\mathcal O_F/\mathfrak p_F^d\to\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p_K^{d'}$ induced by
$F\hookrightarrow K$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$ and put
\[
 q=d+\varepsilon,\qquad q'=d'+\varepsilon',
 \qquad f(y)=N(1+y)-1\quad(y\in\mathfrak p_K^{q'}).
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:stationary-depth-first-inclusion} gives
$f(y)\in\mathfrak p_F^q$.  If $y'-y\in\mathfrak p_K^{m'}$, then
$(1+y')/(1+y)\in U_K^{m'}$, so
\eqref{eq:stationary-depth-second-inclusion} gives
$f(y')\equiv f(y)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^m}$.  Thus $f$ induces the stated map.

For $y,z\in\mathfrak p_K^{q'}$, one has $yz\in\mathfrak p_K^{m'}$ because $2q'\ge m'$.
Multiplicativity of the norm gives the identity
\[
 1+f(y+z+yz)=(1+f(y))(1+f(z)).
\]
The preceding congruence permits replacing $f(y+z+yz)$ by $f(y+z)$
modulo $\mathfrak p_F^m$.  Also $f(y)f(z)\in\mathfrak p_F^{2q}\subseteq\mathfrak p_F^m$.
Hence $f(y+z)\equiv f(y)+f(z)\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^m}$, proving additivity of
$P_{K/F}$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-duality} gives perfectness of both pairings.
For $x\in\mathcal O_F$, the left side of \eqref{eq:Pstar-def} defines a
character of $\mathfrak p_K^{q'}/\mathfrak p_K^{m'}$, depending only on
$\bar x\in\mathcal O_F/\mathfrak p_F^d$.  Perfectness over $K$ gives a unique class
$\bar z\in\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p_K^{d'}$ representing this character.  Character
multiplication and uniqueness make $\bar x\mapsto\bar z$ additive.

Under the stated trace congruence, the left side of
\eqref{eq:Pstar-def} equals
\[
 \psi_F\!\left(\frac{x\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(y)}{\gamma_F}\right)
 =\psi_K(xy/\gamma_F)
 =\psi_K\!\left(\frac{((\gamma_K/\gamma_F)x)y}{\gamma_K}\right).
\]
Since $(\gamma_K/\gamma_F)x\in\mathcal O_K$, uniqueness gives
$P^*_{K/F;\gamma_F,\gamma_K}(\bar x)=\overline{(\gamma_K/\gamma_F)x}$
and its common-denominator specialization.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:stationary-class-under-norm}
