 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)
 =\mathcal R_{\mathrm{odd}}\,
 \left[
 \psi_F(A\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u))\chi_F(z_0)
 \prod_{j\ne0}\tau^j(z_j)
 \right]^{-1}.
\]
Substituting Proposition~\ref{prop:correction-linearization} gives
$\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=\mathcal R_{\mathrm{odd}}\psi_F(-AX)$, with
$X$ as in \eqref{eq:X-def}.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:X-closed}
The element $X$ in \eqref{eq:X-def} satisfies  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:X-closed}
 X=\frac{pB}{1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Put $x_0=z_0-1$ and $x_j=z_j-1$ for $j\ne0$.
For $j\ne0$, multiplication of the conjugates of $u+j$ gives
\[
 N_{K/F}(u+j)=\sum_{r=0}^{p}j^{p-r}s_r,
 \qquad s_0=1,\quad s_p=\mathcal N.
\]
Hence
\[
 x_j=\frac{N_{K/F}(u+j)-(\mathcal N+j)}{\mathcal N+j}
 =\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}j^{p-r}s_r}{\mathcal N+j}.
\]
Because $j^{p-1}=1$,
\begin{equation*}
 \frac1{\mathcal N+j}=
 \frac{\sum_{q=0}^{p-2}(-\mathcal N)^qj^{p-2-q}}
      {1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}.
\end{equation*}
Indeed, multiplying the numerator by $\mathcal N+j$ telescopes to
$1-\mathcal N^{p-1}$.  Using this expansion to sum over the
$(p-1)$ Teichmuller roots, together with
\[
 \sum_{j\ne0}j^r=
 \begin{cases}p-1,&p-1\mid r,\\0,&p-1\nmid r,
 \end{cases}
\]
shows that only the indices $r+q=1$ and $r+q=p$ survive.  With $B=s_1+\sum_{q=1}^{p-2}(-\mathcal N)^q s_{p-q}$, this gives
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{j\ne0}jx_j=\frac{(p-1)B}{1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}.
\end{equation*}

On the other hand,
\[
 N_{K/F}(\mathcal N-u)-(\mathcal N^p-\mathcal N)=\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}(-1)^rs_r\mathcal N^{p-r}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:teichmueller-polynomials},
$z_0=N_{K/F}(\mathcal N-u)/(\mathcal N^p-\mathcal N)$, so
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal N x_0
 &=-\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}(-1)^rs_r\mathcal N^{p-r}}
          {1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}\\
 &=\frac{s_1\mathcal N^{p-1}+\sum_{q=1}^{p-2}(-\mathcal N)^qs_{p-q}}
          {1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}\\
 &=\frac{B}{1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}-s_1.
\end{align*}
Adding $s_1$, this identity, and the formula for $\sum_{j\ne0}jx_j$ above proves
\eqref{eq:X-closed}.  This is an identity in the field $F$ itself.  In
equal characteristic the same finite sums have $p=0$ and $p-1=-1$ in
$F$, so no lifting to characteristic zero is being used.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop:X-depth}
Retain the minimal-conductor choice of $\chi_F$.
One has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:X-depth-final}
 X\in\mathfrak p_F^T,
 \qquad \psi_F(A\mathfrak p_F^T)=1.
\end{equation}
If $\operatorname{char}F=p$, then $X=0$.  In all cases
$\psi_F(-AX)=1$.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
The denominator $1-\mathcal N^{p-1}$ in \eqref{eq:X-closed} is nonzero.  If
$v_F(\mathcal N)\ne0$, this follows from valuations; if $v_F(\mathcal N)=0$,
\eqref{eq:odd-denominator-units} shows that it is a unit.

Suppose first that $\operatorname{char}F=p$.  In \eqref{eq:X-closed}, the integer $p$ is zero in $F$.  Therefore
\[
 X=\frac{pB}{1-\mathcal N^{p-1}}=0,
\]
which proves the first assertion in equal characteristic.

Now assume $\operatorname{char}F=0$.  Put $a=v_K(u)=v_F(\mathcal N)$,
$e=v_F(p)$, and $e_0=\lfloor(p-1)T/p\rfloor=T-\lceil T/p\rceil$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:teichmueller-stationary} gives $e\ge e_0$; for odd $p$,
its proof gives $e_0\ge\lceil T/2\rceil$, hence $2e_0\ge T$.

If $a\ge0$, the denominator in \eqref{eq:X-closed} is a unit, as
shown by \eqref{eq:odd-denominator-units} when $a=0$ and by
$v_F(\mathcal N)>0$ when $a>0$.  By \eqref{eq:symmetric-bound}, every $s_j(u)$ has
valuation at least $e_0$, and the powers of $\mathcal N$ do not decrease it.
Hence $v_F(pB)\ge e+e_0\ge2e_0\ge T$.

If $a<0$, put $c=-a>0$, $y=u^{-1}$, and for
$1\le r\le p-1$ set
\begin{equation*}
 L_r(c)=\left\lfloor \frac{rc+(p-1)T}{p}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation*}
Then $v_F(1-\mathcal N^{p-1})=(p-1)a$, so division by the denominator is
multiplication, up to a unit, by $\mathcal N^{1-p}$.  The reciprocal
identity is
\begin{equation*}
 s_j(u)=\mathcal N\,s_{p-j}(y)\qquad(1\le j\le p-1).
\end{equation*}
Applying this reciprocal identity to the $s_1$ term gives
\[
 v_F\bigl(p\mathcal N^{1-p}s_1(u)\bigr)
 =v_F\bigl(p\mathcal N^{2-p}s_{p-1}(y)\bigr)
 \ge e+(p-2)c+L_{p-1}(c)
 \ge e+e_0\ge T.
\]
For a term $\mathcal N^{p-j}s_j(u)$ with $2\le j\le p-1$,
\[
 v_F\bigl(p\mathcal N^{1-j}s_j(u)\bigr)
 =v_F\bigl(p\mathcal N^{2-j}s_{p-j}(y)\bigr)
 \ge e+(j-2)c+L_{p-j}(c)
 \ge e+e_0\ge T.
\]
Thus $X\in\mathfrak p_F^T$ also in mixed characteristic.

Finally $\tau$ has conductor $T$ and
$\tau(1+x)=\psi_F(Ax)$ on a layer containing $\mathfrak p_F^T$.  Since
$\tau$ is trivial on $1+\mathfrak p_F^T$, one has
$\psi_F(A\mathfrak p_F^T)=1$.  The conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:wild-odd}
For odd $p$, the First Main Lemma holds in  every non-stable wildly ramified case.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Propositions~\ref{prop:odd-phase-cancel} and~\ref{prop:exact-odd-assembly}, together with \eqref{eq:X-depth-final}, give the result.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:quad-X}
Put $s=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)$ and
$X=s+\mathcal N(z_0-1)+(z_1-1)$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quad-zxy}
 z_0-1=-\frac{s}{1+\mathcal N},\qquad
 z_1-1=\frac{s}{1+\mathcal N},\qquad
 X=\frac{2s}{1+\mathcal N}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal N/u$ is the nontrivial conjugate of $u$, the quadratic
norm identity gives
\[
 N_{K/F}(1+u)=1+s+\mathcal N,\qquad
 N_{K/F}(1-\mathcal N/u)=1-s+\mathcal N.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:quad-corrections} proves the first two
identities, and their substitution in the definition of $X$ proves
the third.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lem:quadratic-graded-trace}
Let $K/F$ be wildly ramified quadratic and let
$T=v_K(\mathfrak D_{K/F})=t+1$.  If $r\ge0$ and $r+T$ is odd,
trace induces a $k$-linear isomorphism
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}:\mathfrak p_K^r/\mathfrak p_K^{r+1}
 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
 \mathfrak p_F^{(r+T-1)/2}/\mathfrak p_F^{(r+T+1)/2}.
\]
In particular:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $T$ is odd and $d_\tau=(T-1)/2$, then
$v_F(2)=d_\tau$.  For every $w\in\mathcal O_K^\times$ and every lift
$\widetilde{\bar w}\in\mathcal O_F$ of its residue,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-unit-trace-class}
 \operatorname{Tr}(w)\equiv2\widetilde{\bar w}\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^{d_\tau+1}}.
\end{equation}
\item If $m=2d+1>T$ and $r=m-T$, then trace identifies
$\mathfrak p_K^r/\mathfrak p_K^{r+1}$ with $\mathfrak p_F^d/\mathfrak p_F^{d+1}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
For a quadratic extension, \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} reads
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathfrak p_K^j)=\mathfrak p_F^{\left\lfloor (j+T)/2\right\rfloor}.
\]
If $r+T=2q+1$, then
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathfrak p_K^r)=\mathfrak p_F^q,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathfrak p_K^{r+1})=\mathfrak p_F^{q+1}.
\]
Thus the displayed map induced by trace is surjective.  Both source and target are
one-dimensional $k$-vector spaces, and the map is $k$-linear because
the residue extension is trivial.  It is therefore an isomorphism.

If $T$ is odd, apply the isomorphism with $r=0$.  The class of $1$ is
nonzero and maps to the class of $\operatorname{Tr}(1)=2$, proving
$v_F(2)=d_\tau$.  Since $w-\widetilde{\bar w}\in\mathfrak p_K$, the trace-ideal formula \eqref{eq:trace-ideal}
at $j=1$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(w)-2\widetilde{\bar w}\in\operatorname{Tr}(\mathfrak p_K)
 =\mathfrak p_F^{(T+1)/2}=\mathfrak p_F^{d_\tau+1},
\]
which proves (a).  In particular, a wildly ramified quadratic
extension with $T$ odd is necessarily of mixed characteristic; in
equal characteristic two the equality $v_F(2)=d_\tau$ is impossible.
If $m=2d+1$ and $r=m-T$, then $r+T=m$ and $q=d$, proving (b).
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{lem:normalized-refinement}
Let $h:k\to\mathbf C^\times$ be unimodular and satisfy
$h(r+s)=h(r)h(s)\psi_0(rs)$.
Multiplying $h$ by an additive character gives a unimodular function
$\mathfrak q:k\to\mathbf C^\times$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-refinement}
 \mathfrak q(r+s)=\mathfrak q(r)\mathfrak q(s)\psi_0(rs),
 \qquad
 \mathfrak q(r^2)=\mathfrak q(r).
\end{equation}
Every other function with the same polar character is uniquely
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-linear-family}
 h_\lambda(z)=\mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(\lambda z)
 \qquad(\lambda\in k).
\end{equation}
Write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-normalized-sum}
 H(\lambda)=\operatorname{ph}\!\left(\sum_{z\in k}h_\lambda(z)\right),
 \qquad H_0=H(0).
\end{equation}
We have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-phase-translation}
 H(\lambda)=H_0\overline{\mathfrak q(\lambda)},
 \qquad H_0^2=\mathfrak q(1),
 \qquad \mathfrak q(r)^2=\psi_0(r).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
The quotient
\[
 \ell(z)=\frac{h(z^2)}{h(z)}
\]
is additive.  Indeed, using the defining functional equation for $h$ and Frobenius invariance
of $\psi_0$,
\[
 \ell(r+s)
 =\frac{h((r+s)^2)}{h(r+s)}
 =\frac{h(r^2)}{h(r)}\frac{h(s^2)}{h(s)}
 =\ell(r)\ell(s).
\]
The trace pairing on $k$ is perfect, so there is a unique $c\in k$
such that $\ell(z)=\psi_0(cz)$.  Let $f=[k:\mathbf F_2]$.  For every
$z\in k$, telescoping around the Frobenius orbit gives
\begin{align*}
 1
 &=\frac{h(z^{2^f})}{h(z)}
   =\prod_{i=0}^{f-1}\frac{h(z^{2^{i+1}})}{h(z^{2^i})}\\
 &=\psi_0\!\left(c\sum_{i=0}^{f-1}z^{2^i}\right)
   =\psi_0\!\left(c\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}(z)\right).
\end{align*}
Choose $z$ of absolute trace $1$.  Then $\psi_0(c)=1$, or equivalently
$\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}(c)=0$.

Consider the $\mathbf F_2$-linear map
\[
 L:k\longrightarrow k,
 \qquad L(d)=d+d^{2^{f-1}}.
\]
Writing $\operatorname{Fr}(z)=z^2$, one has
$L=(\operatorname{Fr}-1)\circ\operatorname{Fr}^{-1}$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:frobenius-difference-trace}
therefore gives $\ker L=\mathbf F_2$ and
$\operatorname{im}L=\ker\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}$.  Since $\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}(c)=0$,
there is $d\in k$ such that
\begin{equation*}
 c=d+d^{2^{f-1}}.
\end{equation*}
Replace $h(z)$ by
\[
 \mathfrak q(z)=h(z)\psi_0(dz).
\]
The polar character is unchanged.  Moreover
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\mathfrak q(z^2)}{\mathfrak q(z)}
 &=\psi_0(cz)\psi_0(dz^2+dz)\\
 &=\psi_0\!\left((c+d^{2^{f-1}}+d)z\right)=1,
\end{align*}
where
$\psi_0(dz^2)=\psi_0(d^{2^{f-1}}z)$ and
the displayed choice of $d$ were used.  This proves
$\mathfrak q(z^2)=\mathfrak q(z)$.  If $h'$ has the same polar
character as $\mathfrak q$, then $h'/\mathfrak q$ is an additive
character of $k$, hence is uniquely $z\mapsto\psi_0(\lambda z)$.
This proves \eqref{eq:q-linear-family}.

From \eqref{eq:q-refinement},
\[
 \mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(\lambda z)
 =\mathfrak q(z+\lambda)\mathfrak q(\lambda)^{-1},
\]
so substituting $z\mapsto z+\lambda$ in $\sum_{z\in k}h_\lambda(z)$
gives the first formula in
\eqref{eq:q-phase-translation}.  Setting $r=s$ in
\eqref{eq:q-refinement} gives
\[
 \mathfrak q(r)^2=\psi_0(r^2)=\psi_0(r),
\]
and therefore
$\overline{\mathfrak q(r)}=\mathfrak q(r)\psi_0(r)$.

Put $S_0=\sum_{r\in k}\mathfrak q(r)$.  Its polar bicharacter is
$(r,s)\mapsto\psi_0(rs)$, which is nondegenerate by the perfect trace
pairing.  Equation~\eqref{eq:finite-quadratic-magnitude} therefore gives
\[
 |S_0|^2=|k|,
\]
so $S_0\ne0$.  Finally, translation by $1$ gives
\[
 \overline{S_0}
 =\sum_r\mathfrak q(r)\psi_0(r)
 =\frac1{\mathfrak q(1)}\sum_r\mathfrak q(r+1)
 =\frac{S_0}{\mathfrak q(1)}.
\]
Taking phases yields
$H_0^{-1}=H_0/\mathfrak q(1)$, and hence
$H_0^2=\mathfrak q(1)$.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadratic-critical-functions}
Retain the minimal-conductor choice of $\chi_F$.
For
\[
 \theta\in\{\tau,\chi_F,\tau\chi_F,\chi_K\},
 \qquad
 E_\theta=
 \begin{cases}
  F,&\theta\ne\chi_K,\\
  K,&\theta=\chi_K,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \psi_\theta=
 \begin{cases}
  \psi_F,&\theta\ne\chi_K,\\
  \psi_K,&\theta=\chi_K,
 \end{cases}
\]
if $m_{E_\theta}(\theta)=2d_\theta+1$ is odd, choose an admissible denominator $\gamma_\theta$ and a stationary
representative $\beta_\theta$ from the classes given by
\eqref{eq:low-mu} and Proposition~\ref{prop:low-parameter-table} when
$m\le T$, and by \eqref{eq:wild-two-tau-linearization} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:wild-quadratic-high-parameters} when $m>T$.
Choose a critical element
$\delta_\theta$ with
$\delta_\theta\mathcal O_{E_\theta}=\mathfrak p_{E_\theta}^{d_\theta}$.
The choices can be made so that, for every $z\in k$ and every lift
$\widetilde z\in\mathcal O_F\subset\mathcal O_K$,
\[
 \psi_\theta\!\left(
   \frac{\beta_\theta\delta_\theta^2\widetilde z}
        {\gamma_\theta}\right)=\psi_0(z).
\]
The critical function
$ H_\theta(z)=
 \psi_\theta\!\left(
   \frac{\delta_\theta\beta_\theta\widetilde z}
        {\gamma_\theta}\right)
 \theta(1+\delta_\theta\widetilde z)^{-1}$
then satisfies 
\[
 H_\theta(r+s)=H_\theta(r)H_\theta(s)\psi_0(rs)
 \qquad(r,s\in k).
\]
For even conductor put $H_\theta=1$, in accordance with
\eqref{eq:even-critical-function-constant}.


For each of $\tau,\chi_F,\tau\chi_F,\chi_K$ of odd conductor, the
coefficient in \eqref{eq:q-linear-family} is unique.  Denote these coefficients by
$\gamma_0,\gamma,\gamma_1,\gamma'$, respectively, so that
\[
 H_\tau=h_{\gamma_0},\qquad H_{\chi_F}=h_\gamma,\qquad
 H_{\tau\chi_F}=h_{\gamma_1},\qquad H_{\chi_K}=h_{\gamma'},
\]
with $h_\lambda$ as in \eqref{eq:q-linear-family}.
At $m=T$, put $\rho=\bar u\in k^\times\setminus\{1\}$, and let
$\sqrt\rho$ denote its unique square root in $k$.
These coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-gamma-table}
 (\gamma_1,(\gamma')^2)=
 \begin{cases}
 (\gamma_0,\gamma),&m<T,\\[1mm]
 \left(\dfrac{\gamma_0+\rho\gamma+\sqrt\rho}{1+\rho},\,
       \dfrac{\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho+\sqrt\rho}{1+\rho}\right),&m=T,\\[3mm]
 (\gamma,1+\gamma_0),&m>T.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.  Equations~\eqref{eq:minimal-orbit-conductors},
\eqref{eq:minimal-critical}, and \eqref{eq:pullback-high} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-conductor-table}
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 &m_F(\tau)&m_F(\chi_F)&m_F(\tau\chi_F)&m_K(\chi_K)\\ \hline
 m\le T&T&m&T&m\\
 m>T&T&m&m&2m-T.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
All four conductors are even exactly when $m$ and $T$ are even.

Equation~\eqref{eq:stationary-class-adjoint},
Proposition~\ref{prop:low-parameter-table}, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:wild-quadratic-high-parameters} identify the
stationary classes in the two ranges.  To realize the choices asserted
in the statement, take representatives satisfying the following
equalities, with the parameters \eqref{eq:quadratic-parameters}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-unified-stationary-ratios}
 \frac{\beta(\chi_F)}{\gamma_F}=A\mathcal N,
 \qquad
 \frac{\beta_K}{\gamma_K}=A(\mathcal N-u),
 \qquad \mathcal N=N(u).
\end{equation}
Use the sum representative, relative to a common denominator, for
$\tau\chi_F$.

For an odd-conductor character, form
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function} with the representative just fixed.
Equations~\eqref{eq:Hasse-functional-equation} and
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-residual-character} give a nondegenerate polar
character $\psi_0(cxy)$ with $c\in k^\times$.  Multiplying the
critical element by a unit with residue $c^{-1/2}$ gives the
normalization stated in the proposition, since Frobenius is bijective
on $k$.  For even conductor use $H_\theta=1$, as given by
\eqref{eq:even-critical-function-constant}.
Write the normalized functions for $\tau$ and $\chi_F$ as
$h_{\gamma_0}$ and $h_\gamma$.
At $m=T$, $u$ is a unit and $\overline{\mathcal N}=\rho^2$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:minimal-orbit-no-leading-cancellation}, with $j=1$,
gives $1+\rho^2\ne0$, hence $1+\rho\ne0$.
In the normalized $\delta_\tau$ coordinate, the stationary ratios
$A$ and $A\mathcal N$ give polar characters $\psi_0(xy)$ and
$\psi_0(\rho^2xy)$.  Thus, for a lift
$\widetilde\rho\in\mathcal O_F^\times$, take
$\delta_\chi=\delta_\tau/\widetilde\rho$; the $\chi_F$-function in the
$\delta_\tau$ coordinate is then $h_\gamma(\rho z)$.
The product has polar character $\psi_0((1+\rho)^2xy)$, so its
normalized coordinate is obtained by replacing $z$ by $z/(1+\rho)$.

We first establish the assertions concerning $\tau$, $\chi_F$, and
$\tau\chi_F$, independently of whether $m_K(\chi_K)$ is odd.  Suppose $m<T$ and $T$ is
odd.  Put $d_\tau=(T-1)/2$ and retain the normalized critical element
$\delta_\tau$, of valuation $d_\tau$.  Since
$m<T$,
\[
 d_\tau\ge\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil,
\]
so the stationary linearization of $\chi_F$ is valid on the
$\tau$-critical line.  Choose the sum representative for the
stationary class of $\tau\chi_F$.  Then, for $z\in k$,
\[
 \frac{H_{\tau\chi_F}(z)}{H_\tau(z)}
 =\psi_F(A\mathcal N \delta_\tau\widetilde z)
   \chi_F(1+\delta_\tau\widetilde z)^{-1}=1.
\]
Thus the critical functions of $\tau\chi_F$ and $\tau$ agree, and
$\gamma_1=\gamma_0$.

Suppose $m>T$ and $m$ is odd.  Put $d_\chi=(m-1)/2$ and retain
the normalized critical element $\delta_\chi$, of valuation $d_\chi$.
Since $m>T$,
\[
 d_\chi\ge\left\lceil\frac T2\right\rceil,
\]
so the stationary linearization of $\tau$ is valid on the
$\chi_F$-critical line.  With the sum representative for
$\tau\chi_F$ one obtains
\[
 \frac{H_{\tau\chi_F}(z)}{H_{\chi_F}(z)}
 =\psi_F(A\delta_\chi\widetilde z)
   \tau(1+\delta_\chi\widetilde z)^{-1}=1.
\]
Hence the critical functions of $\tau\chi_F$ and $\chi_F$ agree, and
$\gamma_1=\gamma$.

At the boundary $m=T$, the conductors of $\tau$, $\chi_F$, and
$\tau\chi_F$ are all $T$.  When $T$ is odd, the common-coordinate
convention $\delta_\chi=\delta_\tau/\widetilde\rho$ gives the critical functions
of $\tau$ and $\chi_F$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-boundary-character-functions}
 \mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(\gamma_0z),\qquad
 \mathfrak q(\rho z)\psi_0(\rho\gamma z).
\end{equation}

We now assume that $m_K(\chi_K)$ is odd and compute the critical
function of $\chi_K$.  Let $\delta_K$ be a critical element for $\chi_K$.  For $Z\in k$, choose a
lift $\widetilde Z\in\mathcal O_F$, put
\[
 x_Z=\delta_K\widetilde Z,
 \qquad P(y)=N(1+y)-1=\operatorname{Tr}(y)+N(y),
\]
and put $m_K(\chi_K)=2d_K+1$.  Equation
\eqref{eq:stationary-parameter-ambiguity} gives
$P(x_Z)\in\mathfrak p_F^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}$.  Also
$v_K(ux_Z)\ge a+d_K\ge\lfloor T/2\rfloor$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:graded-norm}(b) gives
$P(ux_Z)\in\mathfrak p_F^{\lfloor T/2\rfloor}$.
Define
\[
 p_{\rm nat}(Z)=\overline{P(x_Z)/\delta_\chi}
 \quad(m\text{ odd}),\qquad
 q_{\rm nat}(Z)=\overline{P(ux_Z)/\delta_\tau}
 \quad(T\text{ odd}).
\]
If $m$ is even, set $p_{\rm nat}=0$; if $T$ is even, set $q_{\rm nat}=0$.

Write $H_K^{\rm nat}(Z)$ for the critical function of $\chi_K$ in
this natural coordinate.  Its definition and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-unified-stationary-ratios} give
\begin{align*}
 H_K^{\rm nat}(Z)
 &=\psi_F\!\left(A\operatorname{Tr}((\mathcal N-u)x_Z)\right)
   \chi_F(1+P(x_Z))^{-1}\\
 &=H_{\chi_F}(p_{\rm nat}(Z))
   \psi_F\!\left(-A\{\operatorname{Tr}(ux_Z)+\mathcal N N(x_Z)\}\right)\\
 &=H_{\chi_F}(p_{\rm nat}(Z))\psi_F(-AP(ux_Z)).
\end{align*}
For the second equality we used the stationary-layer identity
\[
 H_{\chi_F}(p_{\rm nat}(Z))
 =\psi_F(A\mathcal N P(x_Z))\chi_F(1+P(x_Z))^{-1}
\]
and cancelled $\mathcal N\operatorname{Tr}(x_Z)$; the last equality uses
$\mathcal N N(x_Z)=N(ux_Z)$.  Since
$1+P(ux_Z)=N(1+ux_Z)$ and $\tau$ is trivial on norms, the stationary-layer identity for $\tau$ is
\[
 H_\tau(q_{\rm nat}(Z))=\psi_F(AP(ux_Z)).
\]
For odd $T$, \eqref{eq:q-linear-family} and
\eqref{eq:q-phase-translation} give
$H_\tau(q_{\rm nat}(Z))^{-1}
 =H_\tau(q_{\rm nat}(Z))\psi_0(q_{\rm nat}(Z))$.
For even $T$, this also holds because $q_{\rm nat}(Z)=0$ and
$H_\tau\equiv1$.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-exact-transport-natural}
 H_K^{\rm nat}(Z)
 =H_{\chi_F}(p_{\rm nat}(Z))
  H_\tau(q_{\rm nat}(Z))
  \psi_0(q_{\rm nat}(Z)).
\end{equation}

The trace-ideal formula \eqref{eq:trace-ideal} and total ramification give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-critical-trace-norm-bounds}
 v_F(\operatorname{Tr}(\delta_K\widetilde Z))
 \ge\left\lfloor\frac{d_K+T}{2}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad v_F(N(\delta_K\widetilde Z))\ge d_K.
\end{equation}
The norm bound is an equality for $Z\ne0$.
When $m_F(\chi_F)=2d_\chi+1$, $d_K=d_\chi$, and
$\lfloor(d_K+T)/2\rfloor\ge d_\chi+1$, reduction of
$P(\delta_K\widetilde Z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\delta_K\widetilde Z)+N(\delta_K\widetilde Z)$
modulo $\mathfrak p_F^{d_\chi+1}$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-natural-norm-classes}
 p_{\rm nat}(Z)=\lambda_\chi Z^2,
 \qquad\lambda_\chi=\overline{\frac{N(\delta_K)}{\delta_\chi}}\in k^\times.
\end{equation}
When $T=2d_\tau+1$, $a+d_K=d_\tau$, and
$\lfloor(a+d_K+T)/2\rfloor\ge d_\tau+1$, the same reduction of
$P(u\delta_K\widetilde Z)$, with $v_K(u)=a$ and $N(u)=\mathcal N$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-natural-tau-class}
 q_{\rm nat}(Z)=\lambda_\tau Z^2,
 \qquad\lambda_\tau=\overline{\frac{\mathcal N N(\delta_K)}{\delta_\tau}}\in k^\times.
\end{equation}
Both displayed scalars are nonzero when defined.  Replacing $\delta_K$ by
$v_0\delta_K$, with $v_0\in\mathcal O_K^\times$, multiplies both scalars by
$\bar v_0^{\,2}$.  Since Frobenius is an automorphism of $k$, we may
therefore normalize either nonzero scalar to $1$ without changing any
valuation or the ratio of the two scalars.

Put $a=T-m=v_K(u)$.  Suppose first that $m<T$.  Then $m_K=m$, and
when $m$ is odd one has $d_K=d_\chi=(m-1)/2$.  Equations~\eqref{eq:quadratic-critical-trace-norm-bounds} and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-natural-norm-classes} show that
$p_{\rm nat}(Z)=\lambda_\chi Z^2$.  Scale $\delta_K$ so that
$\lambda_\chi=1$.  If $T$ is odd, put $d_\tau=(T-1)/2$.  Since the
odd conductors $m<T$ differ by at least two,
\[
 v_K(u\delta_K)=d_K+a=d_\tau+\frac a2\ge d_\tau+1.
\]
The norm and trace terms of $P(u\delta_K\widetilde Z)$ then lie in
$\mathfrak p_F^{d_\tau+1}$, so $q_{\rm nat}(Z)=0$; if $T$ is even there is no
$\tau$-critical factor.

Suppose next that $m>T$ and that $m_K(\chi_K)$ is odd.  Then
$T$ is odd.  With $d_\tau=(T-1)/2$ and
$m_K=2m-T$, one has
\[
 d_K=m-d_\tau-1,
 \qquad
 v_K(u\delta_K)=a+d_K=d_\tau.
\]
The trace of $u\delta_K\widetilde Z$ lies in
$\mathfrak p_F^{d_\tau+1}$, while its norm has valuation at least $d_\tau$,
with equality for $Z\ne0$; hence
\eqref{eq:quadratic-natural-tau-class} applies.  Scale $\delta_K$ so that
$\lambda_\tau=1$.  If $m$ is odd and $d_\chi=(m-1)/2$, then
\[
 d_K-d_\chi=\frac{m-T}{2}\ge1,
\]
so $P(\delta_K\widetilde Z)$ is beyond the $\chi_F$ critical line; if $m$
is even there is no such critical factor.

Finally suppose $m=T$.  Then $a=0$ and $m_K=m=T$.  When $T$ is odd,
$d_K=d_\chi=d_\tau$.  Both initial terms are norm terms.  Equations
\eqref{eq:quadratic-natural-norm-classes} and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-natural-tau-class} give
\[
 p_{\rm nat}(Z)=\lambda_\chi Z^2,
 \qquad
 q_{\rm nat}(Z)=\lambda_\tau Z^2.
\]
The critical coordinates for $\chi_F$ and $\tau$ were fixed by
$\delta_\chi=\delta_\tau/\widetilde\rho$, and $\overline{\mathcal N}=\rho^2$.  Therefore
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\lambda_\tau}{\lambda_\chi}
 =\overline{\mathcal N}\,\overline{\frac{\delta_\chi}{\delta_\tau}}
 =\rho^2\rho^{-1}=\rho.
\end{equation*}
Scale $\delta_K$ so that $\lambda_\chi=1$.  This single scaling preserves
this ratio, and hence simultaneously
normalizes the two maps to
$p_{\rm nat}(Z)=Z^2$ and $q_{\rm nat}(Z)=\rho Z^2$.
Thus
\[
 (p_{\rm nat}(Z),q_{\rm nat}(Z))=
 \begin{cases}
  (Z^2,0),&m<T,\\
  (Z^2,\rho Z^2),&m=T,\\
  (0,Z^2),&m>T.
 \end{cases}
\]
Define
$H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(z)=H_K^{\rm nat}(z^{1/2})$; this is
well defined because Frobenius is bijective.  Substitution of
the three cases into \eqref{eq:quadratic-exact-transport-natural},
followed by \eqref{eq:q-linear-family}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-raw-functions}
 H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 \mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(\gamma z),&m<T,\\[1mm]
 \mathfrak q(z)\mathfrak q(\rho z)
 \psi_0((\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho)z),&m=T,\\[1mm]
 \mathfrak q(z)\psi_0((1+\gamma_0)z),&m>T.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 H_{\chi_K}(Z)=
 \begin{cases}
 H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(Z^2),&m\ne T,\\[1mm]
 H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(Z^2/(1+\rho)),&m=T.
 \end{cases}
\]
Since $H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(z)=H_K^{\rm nat}(z^{1/2})$, this is
$H_K^{\rm nat}(Z)$ for $m\ne T$ and
$H_K^{\rm nat}(Z/\sqrt{1+\rho})$ for $m=T$.  By the
change-of-critical-element formula following
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function}, the latter is again the critical
function \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function}, with the critical
element rescaled by a unit whose residue is
$(1+\rho)^{-1/2}$.
For $m\ne T$, the raw function has polar quotient $\psi_0(xy)$, which
is unchanged by precomposition with Frobenius.  At $m=T$,
\eqref{eq:q-refinement} gives
\[
 \frac{H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(x+y)}
      {H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(x)H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(y)}
 =\psi_0((1+\rho^2)xy).
\]
Since $1+\rho^2=(1+\rho)^2$ and $1+\rho\ne0$, the function
$Z\mapsto H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(Z^2/(1+\rho))$ has polar quotient
$\psi_0((XY)^2)=\psi_0(XY)$.  Thus $H_{\chi_K}$ has normalized polar character in every case.
Both changes of variable are bijections of $k$, hence
$\sum_{Z\in k}H_{\chi_K}(Z)=\sum_{z\in k}H_{\chi_K}^{\rm raw}(z)$.

At $m=T$, put $r=\sqrt\rho$.  Multiplying the two
functions in \eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-character-functions} and using
\eqref{eq:q-refinement} gives
\[
 \mathfrak q((1+\rho)z)
 \psi_0\bigl((\gamma_0+\rho\gamma)z+\rho z^2\bigr).
\]
Since $\psi_0(\rho z^2)=\psi_0(rz)$, normalization by the coordinate
$(1+\rho)z$ gives the displayed formula for $\gamma_1$.

For the critical function of $\chi_K$ at $m=T$,
the boundary row of \eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-functions} becomes
\[
 \mathfrak q((1+\rho)z)
 \psi_0\bigl((\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho)z+\rho z^2\bigr).
\]
Using $\psi_0(\rho z^2)=\psi_0(rz)$ and substituting
$z\mapsto z/(1+\rho)$ gives the linear coefficient
\[
 L=\frac{\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho+r}{1+\rho}.
\]
The normalized function for $\chi_K$ is obtained by precomposition with
Frobenius.  If $L_0^2=L$, then
\[
 \mathfrak q(z^2)\psi_0(Lz^2)
 =\mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(L_0z),
\]
by \eqref{eq:q-refinement} and Frobenius invariance of the absolute
trace.  Thus Frobenius replaces $L$ by its unique square root
$\gamma'$, so $(\gamma')^2=L$.  Applying the same argument to
the nonboundary rows of \eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-functions} gives
$L=\gamma$ and $L=1+\gamma_0$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:quadratic-gamma-table}.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadratic-residual-quotient}
Retain the setup and notation of
Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic-critical-functions}.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}
 &:=\frac{\Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)\Delta_{3,F}(\tau)}
      {\Delta_{3,F}(\chi_F)\Delta_{3,F}(\tau\chi_F)}\\
 &=\begin{cases}
  1,&m<T\text{ or }m\text{ even},\\[1mm]
  h_\gamma(1)^{-1},&m>T,\ m\text{ odd},\\[1mm]
  h_{\gamma_1+1}\!\left(\dfrac{\rho}{1+\rho}\right),
     &m=T,\ T\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
For odd conductor use the phase $H(\lambda)$ in
\eqref{eq:quadratic-normalized-sum}; for even conductor the factor is
$1$ by \eqref{eq:stationary-factor-definitions}.
Equations~\eqref{eq:q-refinement} and \eqref{eq:q-phase-translation}
give, for $\lambda\in k$,
\[
 H(\lambda)=H(\lambda^2),\qquad
 H(\lambda)^2=\mathfrak q(1)\psi_0(\lambda)=h_\lambda(1),\qquad
 H(1+\lambda)H(\lambda)=1.
\]
For the last identity, \eqref{eq:q-refinement} and
\eqref{eq:q-phase-translation} give
\[
 H(1+\lambda)H(\lambda)
 =H_0^2\overline{\mathfrak q(1+\lambda)}
          \overline{\mathfrak q(\lambda)}=1.
\]

If $m<T$, the conductors in \eqref{eq:quadratic-conductor-table} and
the coefficients in \eqref{eq:quadratic-gamma-table} give
$\Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)=\Delta_{3,F}(\chi_F)$ and
$\Delta_{3,F}(\tau\chi_F)=\Delta_{3,F}(\tau)$.
Thus $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}=1$.

If $m>T$, the product
$\Delta_{3,K}(\chi_K)\Delta_{3,F}(\tau)$ is $1$: for even $T$ both
factors are $1$, and for odd $T$ it is
$H(1+\gamma_0)H(\gamma_0)=1$ by
\eqref{eq:quadratic-gamma-table}.
The denominator is $1$ for even $m$ and is
$H(\gamma)^2=h_\gamma(1)$ for odd $m$.
This proves the asserted formulas when $m>T$.

If $m=T$ and $T$ is even, all four conductors are even, so again
$\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}=1$.

It remains to assume $m=T$ and $T$ odd.  Put
$\rho=\bar u\in k^\times\setminus\{1\}$ and $r=\sqrt\rho$.
All four critical factors are present.  Put
\[
 L=\frac{\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho+r}{1+\rho},
 \qquad A_\rho=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}.
\]
Since $(\gamma')^2=L$, equations~\eqref{eq:q-refinement} and
\eqref{eq:q-phase-translation} give
$H(\gamma')=H_0\overline{\mathfrak q(\gamma')}
=H_0\overline{\mathfrak q(L)}=H(L)$.  Hence
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}
 &=\frac{\overline{\mathfrak q(L)}
          \overline{\mathfrak q(\gamma_0)}}
         {\overline{\mathfrak q(\gamma)}
          \overline{\mathfrak q(\gamma_1)}}\\
 &=\mathfrak q(\gamma)\mathfrak q(\gamma_1)
   \overline{\mathfrak q(L)}\overline{\mathfrak q(\gamma_0)}.
\end{align*}
Set $X_0=\gamma+\gamma_1$ and $Y_0=L+\gamma_0$.  In characteristic
two, substitution of the $m=T$ formulas in \eqref{eq:quadratic-gamma-table} gives
\begin{align*}
 X_0+Y_0
 &=\gamma+\gamma_0
   +\frac{\gamma_0+\rho\gamma+r
          +\gamma+\rho\gamma_0+\rho+r}{1+\rho}\\
 &=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}=A_\rho.
\end{align*}
Thus $X_0=Y_0+A_\rho$.  The refinement law therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}=\mathfrak q(A_\rho)\psi_0(E),
 \qquad
 E=Y_0A_\rho+\gamma\gamma_1+L\gamma_0.
\end{equation*}
Let $a_\rho=r/(1+r)$, so $a_\rho^2=A_\rho$.  An expansion in
characteristic two gives
\begin{equation*}
 E+\gamma_1A_\rho+A_\rho
 =\bigl(a_\rho(\gamma+\gamma_0)+A_\rho\bigr)^2
  +\bigl(a_\rho(\gamma+\gamma_0)+A_\rho\bigr).
\end{equation*}
The right side of this identity has
absolute trace zero. Substituting this into
$\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}=\mathfrak q(A_\rho)\psi_0(E)$ gives
\[
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}=\mathfrak q(A_\rho)
      \psi_0(\gamma_1A_\rho+A_\rho)=h_{\gamma_1+1}(A_\rho).
\]

This proves \eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient}.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{lem:quadratic-correction-depth}
The correction units in \eqref{eq:quad-corrections} satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-correction-depth-bound}
 v_F(z_0-1)=v_F(z_1-1)
 \ge\left\lfloor\frac{T+|a|}{2}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
Put $s=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)$.  Since
$v_F(1+\mathcal N)=\min\{a,0\}$, equations~\eqref{eq:quad-zxy} and
\eqref{eq:trace-ideal} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_F(z_0-1)=v_F(z_1-1)
 &=v_F(s)-\min\{a,0\}\\
 &\ge\left\lfloor\frac{a+T}{2}\right\rfloor-\min\{a,0\}
  =\left\lfloor\frac{T+|a|}{2}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadratic-correction-values}
Retain the setup and notation of
Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic-critical-functions}.   One has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-correction-values}
\begin{aligned}
 &\bigl(\psi_F(A\mathcal N(z_0-1))\chi_F(z_0)^{-1},\,
        \psi_F(A(z_1-1))\tau(z_1)^{-1}\bigr)\\
 &\qquad=\begin{cases}
 (1,1),&m<T\text{ or }m\text{ even},\\[1mm]
 (h_\gamma(1),1),&m>T,\ m\text{ odd},\\[1mm]
 \left(h_\gamma\!\left(\dfrac{\rho^2}{1+\rho^2}\right),\,
       h_{\gamma_0}\!\left(\dfrac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}\right)\right),
       &m=T,\ T\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}$.
Put $x=z_0-1$ and $y=z_1-1$.
For a character $\theta$ of $F^\times$ of odd conductor
$2d_\theta+1$, write $H_\theta=h_\lambda$ using its normalized
critical element $\delta_\theta$.
Substitution of the lift $w/\delta_\theta$ in
\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-residual-correction}
 \theta(1+w)^{-1}
 =\psi_F\!\left(-\frac{\beta_\theta w}{\gamma_\theta}\right)
  h_\lambda\!\left(\overline{w/\delta_\theta}\right)
 \qquad(w\in\mathfrak p_F^{d_\theta}).
\end{equation}
Since $m=T-a$, the bound \eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-depth-bound}
is at least both $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ and $\lfloor T/2\rfloor$.
Thus \eqref{eq:quadratic-residual-correction} applies to
$(\theta,w)=(\chi_F,x)$ and $(\tau,y)$ when the respective conductor
is odd.  For even conductor, the bound reaches the linearization
domain in \eqref{eq:quadratic-linearization-domains}.
For odd conductor put
$x'=\overline{x/\delta_\chi}$ or $y'=\overline{y/\delta_\tau}$,
respectively.  The two residual factors are $h_\gamma(x')$ and
$h_{\gamma_0}(y')$; for even conductor the respective factor is $1$.

For a fixed stationary representative, normalized critical elements
give the same critical function.  Indeed, if $\delta_\theta'=v\delta_\theta$
with $v\in\mathcal O_F^\times$, their normalization implies
$\psi_0((\bar v^2-1)z)=1$ for every $z\in k$.
Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing gives $\bar v^2=1$, hence $\bar v=1$.
By \eqref{eq:Lamprecht-Hasse-function},
$H_\theta'(z)=H_\theta(\bar v z)=H_\theta(z)$.

If $m<T$, the bound \eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-depth-bound} is
at least $(m+1)/2$ when $m$ is odd and at least $(T+1)/2$ when $T$
is odd.  Thus $x'=y'=0$ whenever defined, and both residual factors
are $1$.

Suppose $m>T$.  When $T$ is odd,
\eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-depth-bound} gives
$v_F(y)\ge\lfloor m/2\rfloor\ge(T+1)/2$, so $y'=0$.
When $T$ is even, \eqref{eq:quadratic-linearization-domains} applies
to $y$.  Thus the $\tau$ residual factor is always $1$.
For even $m$, the same linearization applies to $x$, proving the
asserted pair $(1,1)$.

Now suppose $m>T$ and $m$ is odd.  Put $c=m-T>0$ and $w=u^{-1}$.  Then $v_K(w)=c$ and
$c+T=m$ is odd.  Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-graded-trace}(b) shows that
\[
 \delta_\chi:=-\operatorname{Tr}(w)\in\mathfrak p_F^{(m-1)/2}\setminus\mathfrak p_F^{(m+1)/2}
\]
is a valid critical element for $\chi_F$.  We verify the required normalization.  Since
\[
 v_F(\mathcal N\delta_\chi^2)=(T-m)+(m-1)=T-1,
\]
the map
\[
 z\longmapsto\psi_F(A\mathcal N\delta_\chi^2\widetilde z)
\]
is the nontrivial character induced by $\tau$ on
$U_F^{T-1}/U_F^T$.  Indeed, $T\ge2$ and hence
$T-1\ge\lceil T/2\rceil$, so the stationary linearization of $\tau$
is valid on $U_F^{T-1}$; nontriviality follows from the exact conductor
$T$ of $\tau$.

Put
\[
 r=\frac{w}{\operatorname{Tr}(w)}.
\]
Then $\operatorname{Tr}(r)=1$ and, since $N(w)=\mathcal N^{-1}$,
\[
 N(r)=\frac{N(w)}{\operatorname{Tr}(w)^2}
     =\frac1{\mathcal N \delta_\chi^2},
 \qquad
 N(r)^{-1}=\mathcal N \delta_\chi^2.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 v_K(r)=v_K(w)-v_K(\operatorname{Tr}(w))
       =(m-T)-(m-1)=1-T.
\]
For every $z\in k$ and every lift $\widetilde z\in\mathcal O_F$, the element
$1+(\widetilde z/N(r))r$ is a unit of $K$: indeed,
\[
 v_K\!\left(\frac{\widetilde z}{N(r)}r\right)
 \ge 2(T-1)+(1-T)=T-1>0.
\]
The quadratic norm identity therefore gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 N\!\left(1+\frac{\widetilde z}{N(r)}r\right)
 &=1+\frac{\widetilde z}{N(r)}\operatorname{Tr}(r)
      +\frac{\widetilde z^{\,2}}{N(r)^2}N(r)\\
 &=1+\mathcal N \delta_\chi^2\bigl(\widetilde z+\widetilde z^{\,2}\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since $\tau$ is trivial on norms, its stationary linearization gives
\[
 \psi_F\!\left(A\mathcal N\delta_\chi^2
       (\widetilde z+\widetilde z^{\,2})\right)=1\qquad(z\in k).
\]
By \eqref{eq:scaled-frobenius-trace-image}, with $p=2$ and
$\lambda=1$, the image of $z\mapsto z^2+z$ is $\ker\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}$.
The displayed character is therefore a nontrivial character of the
quotient $k/\ker\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}\simeq\mathbf F_2$, hence is $\psi_0$.
Consequently
\[
 \psi_F(A\mathcal N \delta_\chi^2\widetilde z)=\psi_0(z).
\]
Hence $\delta_\chi=-\operatorname{Tr}(w)$ gives the normalized polar character.
Put $s=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)$.  Since
\[
 \frac{s}{\mathcal N}=\operatorname{Tr}(u^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}(w)
\]
and $x=-s/(1+\mathcal N)$, one has the identity
\[
 \frac{x}{\delta_\chi}=\frac{\mathcal N}{1+\mathcal N}
 =1-\frac1{1+\mathcal N}.
\]
Here $v_F(\mathcal N)=T-m=-c$, so $v_F((1+\mathcal N)^{-1})=c>0$.  Therefore the
normalized correction class is
\begin{equation*}
 x'=\overline{x/\delta_\chi}=1.
\end{equation*}
Equation~\eqref{eq:quadratic-residual-correction} therefore gives
the residual factor $h_\gamma(1)$, proving the case $m>T$, $m$ odd.

If $m=T$ and $T$ is even, the bound
\eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-depth-bound} gives $x,y\in\mathfrak p_F^{T/2}$,
so \eqref{eq:quadratic-linearization-domains} gives the pair $(1,1)$.

Finally suppose $m=T$ and $T$ is odd.  Put
$\rho=\bar u$, $s=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)$, and $d_\tau=(T-1)/2$.
Choose a lift $\widetilde\rho\in\mathcal O_F^\times$ of $\rho$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-graded-trace}(a) gives $v_F(2)=d_\tau$, so
\[
 \delta_\tau=2,\qquad \delta_\chi=2/\widetilde\rho
\]
are critical elements for $\tau$ and $\chi_F$, respectively.
We verify the normalization of $\delta_\tau=2$.
Since $T$ is odd and $m=T>1$, one has $T\ge3$.  Hence
$T-1\ge\lceil T/2\rceil$, so the stationary linearization of $\tau$
is valid on $4\mathcal O_F$.  Since $\delta_\tau=2$ and $v_F(4)=T-1$, the map
\[
 z\longmapsto\psi_F(A\delta_\tau^2\widetilde z)
             =\tau(1+4\widetilde z)
\]
is the character induced by $\tau$ on
$U_F^{T-1}/U_F^T$.  It is nontrivial because $\tau$ has exact
conductor $T$.  For every $z\in k$, the element $1+2\widetilde z$
lies in $F^\times\subset K^\times$, and hence
\[
 N(1+2\widetilde z)
 =(1+2\widetilde z)^2
 =1+4(\widetilde z+\widetilde z^{\,2}).
\]
The character $\tau$ is trivial on norms, so its stationary
linearization gives
\[
 \psi_F\!\left(A\delta_\tau^2
       (\widetilde z+\widetilde z^{\,2})\right)=1.
\]
By \eqref{eq:scaled-frobenius-trace-image}, with $p=2$ and
$\lambda=1$, the image of $z\mapsto z^2+z$ is $\ker\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}$.
The displayed character is nontrivial on
$k/\ker\operatorname{Tr}_{k/\mathbf F_2}\simeq\mathbf F_2$, so it is $\psi_0$.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-boundary-polar-normalization}
 \psi_F(A\delta_\tau^2\widetilde z)=\psi_0(z)
 \qquad(z\in k).
\end{equation}
Since $\overline{\mathcal N}=\rho^2$,
\eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-polar-normalization} gives
\[
 \psi_F(A\mathcal N\delta_\chi^2\widetilde z)
 =\psi_F\!\left(4A\frac{\mathcal N}{\widetilde\rho^{\,2}}
                    \widetilde z\right)=\psi_0(z).
\]
Thus these choices give the normalized functions $h_{\gamma_0}$ and
$h_\gamma$ already fixed in Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic-critical-functions}.

Since $u-\widetilde\rho\in\mathfrak p_K$, the unit-trace congruence
\eqref{eq:quadratic-unit-trace-class} gives
\[
 s-2\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(u-\widetilde\rho)\in\mathfrak p_F^{d_\tau+1}.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation*}
 \overline{s/\delta_\tau}=\rho.
\end{equation*}
Combining $\overline{s/\delta_\tau}=\rho$,
\eqref{eq:quad-zxy}, and $\overline{\mathcal N}=\rho^2$, where
$\rho=\bar u$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-boundary-correction-classes}
 x'=\overline{x/\delta_\chi}=\frac{\rho^2}{1+\rho^2},
 \qquad
 y'=\overline{y/\delta_\tau}=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}.
\end{equation}
Substituting \eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-correction-classes} in
\eqref{eq:quadratic-residual-correction} proves the remaining case of
\eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-values}.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadratic-complete-assembly}
Retain the minimal-conductor choice of $\chi_F$.
With $X$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:quad-X},
$\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}$ from
\eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient}, and $\rho=\bar u$ when $m=T$,
the error quotient satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-assembly}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)
 &=\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}\,\psi_F(-AX)\\[-1mm]
 &\quad\times\begin{cases}
  1,&m<T\text{ or }m\text{ even},\\[1mm]
  h_\gamma(1),&m>T,\ m\text{ odd},\\[1mm]
  h_\gamma\!\left(\dfrac{\rho^2}{1+\rho^2}\right)
  h_{\gamma_0}\!\left(\dfrac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}\right),
    &m=T,\ T\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
Write $N=N_{K/F}$.  Use \eqref{eq:Delta-factorization-new},
\eqref{eq:trivial-local-constant}, and the following admissible denominators and stationary representatives.
Rescaling a denominator and its numerator uses
Lemma~\ref{lem:stationary-class-calculus}(b).
For $m>T$, the pairs and their sources are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \text{character}&(\gamma_\theta,\beta_\theta)&\text{source}\\ \hline
 \chi_K&(\gamma_F,\ \alpha\delta_h(\mathcal N-u))
  &\eqref{eq:Pstar-wild-two}\\
 \tau&(\gamma_F/(\alpha\delta_h),\ 1)
  &\eqref{eq:wild-two-tau-linearization}\\
 \chi_F&(\gamma_F,\ \alpha\delta_h\mathcal N)
  &\eqref{eq:Lamprecht-linearization},\ \eqref{eq:quadratic-parameters}\\
 \tau\chi_F&(\gamma_F,\ \alpha\delta_h(\mathcal N+1))
  &\eqref{eq:Pstar-wild-two}.
\end{array}
\]
For $m\le T$, they are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \text{character}&(\gamma_\theta,\beta_\theta)&\text{source}\\ \hline
 \chi_K&(\Gamma_\tau/\xi_1,\ (\alpha/\xi_1)(\mathcal N-u))
  &\text{Proposition~\ref{prop:low-parameter-table}}\\
 \tau&(\Gamma_\tau/\alpha,\ 1)&\eqref{eq:low-mu}\\
 \chi_F&(\Gamma_\tau/\xi,\ (\alpha/\xi)\mathcal N)
  &\eqref{eq:gammas-low},\ \eqref{eq:low-mu}\\
 \tau\chi_F&(\Gamma_\tau,\ \alpha(\mathcal N+1))
  &\eqref{eq:low-beta-twists}\ (j=1).
\end{array}
\]
The factors contributed by the admissible elements are, in the high
range,
\[
 \frac{\chi_K(\gamma_F)\tau(\gamma_F/(\alpha\delta_h))}
      {\chi_F(\gamma_F)(\tau\chi_F)(\gamma_F)}
 =\tau(\alpha\delta_h)^{-1},
\]
and in the low range,
\[
 \frac{\chi_K(\Gamma_\tau/\xi_1)\tau(\Gamma_\tau/\alpha)}
      {\chi_F(\Gamma_\tau/\xi)(\tau\chi_F)(\Gamma_\tau)}
 =\tau(\alpha)^{-1}=1.
\]
Here $\chi_K=\chi_F\circ N$, $N(\xi_1)=\xi$, and $\alpha$ is a norm.

It remains to collect the factors $\theta(\beta)^{-1}$ from
\eqref{eq:stationary-factor-definitions}.  In the high range they give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\chi_K\!\left(\alpha\delta_h(\mathcal N-u)\right)^{-1}
  \chi_F(\alpha\delta_h\mathcal N)
  (\tau\chi_F)\!\left(\alpha\delta_h(\mathcal N+1)\right)\\
 &\qquad=\tau(\alpha\delta_h)\,
  \chi_F\!\left(\frac{\mathcal N(\mathcal N+1)}{N(\mathcal N-u)}\right)
  \tau(\mathcal N+1)=\tau(\alpha\delta_h)H,
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
 H=\chi_F\!\left(\frac{\mathcal N(\mathcal N+1)}{N(\mathcal N-u)}\right)
   \tau(\mathcal N+1).
\]
Indeed, $N(\alpha\delta_h)=(\alpha\delta_h)^2$, so the scalar factors
in the two $\chi_F$-values cancel that in the $\chi_K$-value.
The low-range contribution is
\[
 \chi_K\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{\xi_1}(\mathcal N-u)\right)^{-1}
 \chi_F\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{\xi}\mathcal N\right)
 (\tau\chi_F)\!\left(\alpha(\mathcal N+1)\right)=H,
\]
because $N(\alpha/\xi_1)=\alpha^2/\xi$ and $\tau(\alpha)=1$.
Multiplication by the admissible-element quotients therefore leaves
$H$ in both ranges; in particular the high-range factor
$\tau(\alpha\delta_h)$ cancels its inverse.

By \eqref{eq:quad-corrections},
\[
 \mathcal N-u=-u(1-\mathcal N/u),\qquad
 N(\mathcal N-u)=\mathcal N N(1-\mathcal N/u)
               =\mathcal N(1+\mathcal N)z_0.
\]
Also $N(1+u)=(1+\mathcal N)z_1$, and $\tau$ is trivial on norms.
Consequently
\[
 H=\chi_F(z_0)^{-1}\tau(z_1)^{-1}.
\]

Since $\psi_K=\psi_F\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}$, the additive stationary values
have signed sum
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(\mathcal N-u)+1-\mathcal N-(\mathcal N+1)
 =-\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u).
\]
Together with $H$ and the residual quotient
\eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient}, this gives
\[
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=\mathcal R_{\mathrm{even}}\,
 \left[\psi_F(A\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u))\chi_F(z_0)\tau(z_1)\right]^{-1}.
\]
Substitute \eqref{eq:quadratic-correction-values}.  The additive
arguments combine as
\[
 -A\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)+\mathcal N(z_0-1)+(z_1-1)\bigr)=-AX
\]
by the definition of $X$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:quad-X}.
This proves \eqref{eq:quadratic-assembly}.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadratic-norm-trace-phase}
Retain the minimal-conductor choice of $\chi_F$ and $X$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:quad-X}.
If $\operatorname{char}F=2$, then $X=0$.
If $\operatorname{char}F=0$ and either $m\ne T$ or $T$ is even, then
$X\in\mathfrak p_F^T$.
With $\rho=\bar u$ when $m=T$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-norm-trace-phase}
 \psi_F(-AX)=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&m\ne T\text{ or }T\text{ even},\\[1mm]
  \psi_0\!\left(\dfrac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}\right),&m=T,\ T\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:quadratic-linearization-domains} gives
$\psi_F(A\mathfrak p_F^T)=1$, since $\tau$ has conductor $T$.
If $\operatorname{char}F=2$, then $T$ is even: otherwise
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-graded-trace}(a) would give
$v_F(2)=(T-1)/2$, although $2=0$ in $F$.
Thus the break $t=T-1$ is odd, and \eqref{eq:quad-zxy} gives $X=0$.
This proves the assertions in characteristic two.

Assume $\operatorname{char}F=0$.  Put $e=v_F(2)$ and
$s=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(u)$.  Since $2=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(1)$, the trace-ideal formula
\eqref{eq:trace-ideal} gives
\[
 e\ge\left\lfloor\frac T2\right\rfloor,\qquad
 v_F(s)\ge\left\lfloor\frac{a+T}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
If $a>0$, then $1+\mathcal N$ is a unit, and \eqref{eq:quad-zxy} gives
\[
 v_F(X)\ge e+\left\lfloor\frac{a+T}{2}\right\rfloor\ge T.
\]
If $a<0$, put $c=-a>0$.  Since $v_F(1+\mathcal N)=-c$,
\[
 v_F(X)\ge e+\left\lfloor\frac{T-c}{2}\right\rfloor+c
          =e+\left\lfloor\frac{T+c}{2}\right\rfloor\ge T.
\]
If $a=0$ and $T$ is even, $1+\mathcal N$ is a unit and the bound is
$e+T/2\ge T$.  Thus $X\in\mathfrak p_F^T$ and $\psi_F(-AX)=1$ in all these
cases.

It remains to take $m=T$ and $T$ odd.  Put
$\rho=\bar u$, $C=\rho/(1+\rho^2)$, and $y=z_1-1$.
The critical element in \eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-polar-normalization}
is $\delta_\tau=2$, and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-correction-classes} gives
$y/2\equiv C\pmod{\mathfrak p_F}$.
By \eqref{eq:quad-zxy}, $X=2y$; since $v_F(4)=T-1$, it follows that
\[
 X\equiv4\widetilde C\pmod{\mathfrak p_F^T}
\]
for any lift $\widetilde C\in\mathcal O_F$ of $C$.
Using $\psi_F(A\mathfrak p_F^T)=1$ and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-boundary-polar-normalization}, we obtain
\[
 \psi_F(-AX)=\psi_0(-C)=\psi_0(C),
\]
because $k$ has characteristic two.  This proves
\eqref{eq:quadratic-norm-trace-phase}.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{prop:wild-quadratic-cancellation}
For every wildly ramified quadratic extension $K/F$ of nonarchimedean
local fields and every quasi-character $\chi_F$ of $F^\times$,
\[
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=1.
\]
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:error-twist-invariance}, choose $\chi_F$ of minimal
conductor in its $S(K/F)$-orbit.  Conductors $0$ and $1$ were treated
in Subsection~\ref{sec:wild-endpoints}, so assume $m_F(\chi_F)>1$.

If $m<T$ or $m$ is even, both the residual quotient in
\eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient} and the additional factor in
\eqref{eq:quadratic-assembly} are $1$.
If $m>T$ and $m$ is odd, those factors are $h_\gamma(1)^{-1}$ and
$h_\gamma(1)$, respectively, and cancel.
Thus, whenever $m\ne T$ or $T$ is even,
\eqref{eq:quadratic-assembly} and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-norm-trace-phase} give
$\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=\psi_F(-AX)=1$.

Suppose $m=T$ and $T$ is odd.  Put
\[
  r=\sqrt\rho,\qquad
 A_\rho=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho},\qquad
 B=\frac{\rho^2}{1+\rho^2},\qquad C=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}.
\]
Equations~\eqref{eq:quadratic-raw-Hasse-quotient},
\eqref{eq:quadratic-assembly}, and
\eqref{eq:quadratic-norm-trace-phase}, with
$h_\lambda(z)=\mathfrak q(z)\psi_0(\lambda z)$, give
\[
 \mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)
 =\mathfrak q(A_\rho)\mathfrak q(B)\mathfrak q(C)
  \psi_0(\gamma_1A_\rho+\gamma B+\gamma_0C+C+A_\rho).
\]
Since $B+C=A_\rho$, the refinement identity \eqref{eq:q-refinement} gives
\[
 \mathfrak q(B)\mathfrak q(C)
 =\mathfrak q(A_\rho)\psi_0(BC),
 \qquad BC=\frac{\rho^3}{1+\rho^4}.
\]
Substitution in the expression for $\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)$, using
$\mathfrak q(A_\rho)^2=\psi_0(A_\rho)$, gives
$\mathcal E_{K/F}(\chi_F)=\psi_0(a_2)$ with
\[
 a_2=\gamma_1A_\rho+\gamma B+\gamma_0C+C
      +\frac{\rho^3}{1+\rho^4}.
\]
Substituting the $m=T$ value from \eqref{eq:quadratic-gamma-table},
$\gamma_1=(\gamma_0+\rho\gamma+r)/(1+\rho)$ cancels the terms in
$\gamma$ and $\gamma_0$ and gives
\begin{equation*}
 a_2
 =\frac{\rho^3}{(1+\rho^2)^2}
  +\frac{\rho(1+r)}{(1+\rho)^2}.
\end{equation*}
The first term on the right is the square of
$r^3/(1+\rho^2)$.  Frobenius invariance of $\psi_0$ therefore reduces
its phase to that of
\[
 a_4=\frac{r^3}{1+\rho^2}
     +\frac{\rho(1+r)}{(1+\rho)^2}
     =\frac{\rho}{1+\rho^2}
     =\frac{\rho}{(1+\rho)^2}.
\]
With $c=(1+\rho)^{-1}$, $a_4=c+c^2$, so
  $\psi_0(a_4)=1$ by \eqref{eq:AS-phase}.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Let $F$ be a nonarchimedean local field and let $K/F$ be cyclic of
prime degree $\ell$.  If $K/F$ is unramified, apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:unramified-new}.  If it is ramified and tame, the odd-degree and quadratic cases are
Propositions~\ref{prop:tame-odd-new} and
\ref{prop:tame-two-new}.

Suppose that $K/F$ is wild.  Then $\ell=p$, the residue
characteristic.  By \eqref{eq:error-twist-invariance}, replace $\chi_F$ by a
member of minimal conductor in its $S(K/F)$-orbit.  Conductors $0$ and
$1$ are treated in Subsection~\ref{sec:wild-endpoints}.  For odd $p$,
the stable range is Proposition~\ref{prop:wild-stable-new}, and the
remaining non-stable range is Corollary~\ref{cor:wild-odd}.  For
$p=2$, we have Proposition \ref{prop:wild-quadratic-cancellation}.  These cases
exhaust all cyclic extensions of prime degree.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
